questions.title: Where is Broxtowe House, and why does a Park Valley schedule carry the name?
questions.detail:
**Settled: the Park Valley household is at 6 Park Valley.** Mary Enfield, 79, her brother Henry, 71, an artist, her companion Jane Chaffer and two servants are filed at Stuart Cottage (#262) on the 1921 return, and A. Hagues confirms the house. Their census rows now carry that address and a source.

**Their schedule is addressed Broxtowe House, and that is not accepted as a name for the house.** A. Hagues cannot see 6 Park Valley as Broxtowe House, so no such name is recorded against #262 and none should be. The address on that schedule is therefore unexplained: an enumerator's or indexer's error, a postal usage that did not belong to the building, or something else. Understanding where it came from is now part of this question rather than evidence for a second house.

**An earlier draft of this question went further than the evidence.** It reasoned first that Stuart Cottage could not be a candidate because it has a name and a listed description of its own, and then, once the household was confirmed there, that the name must have been carried by two houses. Neither conclusion is kept. What is known is narrower: the household is at 6 Park Valley, and its schedule says Broxtowe House.

**The Park Terrace end, which is where the name belongs.** Dr Kneebone's 1921 schedule gives his postal address as 'Broxtow House, The Park', spelt without the e, and his household falls between 19 Park Terrace and Sunnyside. Alfred Bradley, a single cotton doubler of 45, with his niece, a visiting governess and three servants, is returned at Broxtowe House on the 1891 census and is filed at **#406**, between 1 and 3 Park Terrace in that year's walk. On A. Hagues's instruction Kneebone (#1843) is being filed at #406 as well.

**What is still wanted: which building #406 is.** It is a census-only property - no description, no build date, no position beyond the walk order - and it now carries two households thirty years apart. 20 Park Terrace holds no census record at all and remains a candidate for the same ground. The name appears **nowhere in any directory volume, in any spelling**. A rate book, a deed, or an older map would settle it, and might also explain the Park Valley schedule.

questions.title: Which hospital did the nine doctors at Broxtowe House serve?
questions.detail: Nine house surgeons and house physicians, aged 26 to 33, living in one Park house in June 1921 with no patients and no family. Nottingham General Hospital at Standard Hill is the obvious answer on geography alone, and the hospital's own history records it taking houses in The Park, Park Terrace and the Ropewalk as doctors' residences — but dates that to 1969. If a hospital minute book, annual report or staff list names the residence, it would push the practice back nearly fifty years. Five of the nine were women, which in 1921 makes the house worth a note in its own right.

questions.title: Where did the Carr household live in 1921?
questions.detail: Three separate schedules were filed under 19 Park Terrace in the 1921 census: the Clark household (19 Park Terrace itself), the nine doctors at Broxtowe House, and Arthur Carr with his wife, a son of three, a visitor and three servants. The Carrs need a house. The enumerator's round puts them between Broxtowe House and Sunnyside. 20 Park Terrace is empty in the record for that year, and Sunnyside itself already holds two schedules.

questions.title: Which houses did the Weinberg and Smith families live in?
questions.detail: Twenty-two people were filed under 9 Cavendish Crescent North in the 1911 census, which is three schedules, not one household. Four servants with no head belong to Peveril House itself — Weston Fulford Marriott Weston-Webb held the lease and signed the return without being there on the night. The other two are the Weinbergs (nine people, head a shipping merchant and lace manufacturer) and the Smiths (nine people, head a lace manufacturer). The enumerator ran 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 up the crescent, and 10, 11 (Gleadthorpe) and 12 all hold no 1911 record, so the next two houses along are the candidates.

questions.title: Which house on Huntingdon Drive is Greendale? — answered: 4
questions.detail: Settled by A. Hagues: Joseph Spray's biography gives his address as Greendale, Huntingdon Drive, The Park, and Companies House records put Greendale at 4 Huntingdon Drive. The record already linked the Sprays to number 4 from 1911. 4 Huntingdon Drive now carries the name; press Record what you found to close this.

questions.title: Belwood is the corner of Tattershall Drive and Tennis Drive — which households were in it?
questions.detail: Found, or as near as makes no difference. A. Hagues has it on the street: a house at the Tattershall Drive corner with Tennis Drive carries BELWOOD on the post beside its door. The Land Registry postcodes agree — Belwood and Ellington are both NG7 1AD, along with the four flats at Tennis View, while Park Lodge and The Lodge sit apart in NG7 1BX. Ellington House (#312) is already in the record at that end of the street, so Belwood is its neighbour. What stands there now is modern: brick, flat-roofed, tall narrow windows, later 20th century by the look of it, so whatever Dougal de Havilland and the OS sheets recorded has gone and the name was carried over to its replacement. That is worth saying carefully — the name on a modern door is evidence of the site, not proof that the old house stood on the same footprint. What is still wanted is a household. No census entry anywhere in the record names Belwood, or any address on Tattershall Drive, so under this record's rule it stays a name rather than a property until somebody is found living in it. Dougal's map puts Belwood at x 174.0, y 403.3 with Hazelwood beside it at x 187.0, y 408.7 — the map's own coordinates, which nothing in the record can yet turn into a position on the ground.

questions.title: Penrhyn Cottage and Penrhyn House — one building or two?
questions.detail: The record holds Penrhyn House on Clumber Road East. Penrhyn Cottage turns up separately. Is the cottage the same building under an earlier or a smaller name, a lodge or coach house in its grounds, or a different building altogether? The Park has a number of coach houses turned into cottages and given their own name — Gartree Lodge is one — so a second building is entirely plausible.

questions.title: Gartree Lodge: standing, at 17a Tattershall Drive, and where the map puts it
questions.detail: Both halves answered on the ground by A. Hagues. It stands, it is 17a Tattershall Drive, and it goes by The Lodge now — which is why HM Land Registry's unnumbered "The Lodge" on this street is this house and not the lodge beside the tennis ground. And the position was right: he took the point this record already held, looked at it on Street View, and found the building exactly there. That point had been a calculated guess — the Tattershall Drive end of Gartree House's garden, 28m short of 4 Tattershall Drive along the line between them — so it is worth saying that the guess has been checked rather than merely left standing. The house began as part of the carriage and stable building at the bottom of Gartree House's garden, converted into a separate dwelling and addressed on the street the garden backs onto. In 1921 it held John Raven Erwin Hatton, a chauffeur of 28, and his wife Evelyn, 22 — a chauffeur housed over the stables of the house he drove for. Nothing here is open any longer; mark it answered on this page when you are ready, since an answer belongs to whoever made it rather than to the seed file.

questions.title: Is there a house at 14 Huntingdon Drive?
questions.detail: The 1921 census records Sidney Richard Tann, a chiropodist of 42, and his wife Daisy at "Huntingdon Drive (The Cottage)". The road is otherwise recorded only as far as number 10, so the number 14 is a guess and the house may no longer stand. Does anything of it survive, and where was it?

questions.title: Where exactly does The Hermitage stand?
questions.detail: Two positions are held for The Hermitage and they are 48 metres apart — one placed by hand, one derived. Nothing turns on it except the map, but on a site this small 48 metres is the difference between one building and its neighbour.

questions.title: What was Clumber Court?
questions.detail: Recorded as demolished, with no residents linked to it and no census year at all. Either the links have gone missing or the record was never more than a stub. What stood there, when did it go, and did anyone in the record live in it?

questions.title: Peveril House or Peveril Tower — which name, and when?
questions.detail: 9 Cavendish Crescent North is recorded under both names, and there is a second Peveril House on Peveril Drive. Which name did the Cavendish Crescent house carry, and over what period? The name clash is a live risk: a census address reading only "Peveril House" could be filed against either.

questions.title: What is the colour key on Dougal de Havilland's map?
questions.detail: The map colours the houses, and the colouring appears to encode the architect or the building period. Reading it off the scan gave forty suggestions that all fell into a single class, which is almost certainly wrong — the yellow road markings were being read as the yellow of one of the periods. Does a printed key exist, or does anyone remember what the colours meant? With the key, the map would name the architect of a great many houses at once.

questions.title: 171 names on Dougal's map have no house in the record
questions.detail: Mining the map turned up 964 labels. 86 matched a property outright; 171 are house-shaped names with nothing behind them. Some will be subdivisions and flats, some earlier names of houses already held, and some genuinely missing. Working the list down is the single largest source of new house names available, and most of it can be done from an armchair by anyone who knows the estate.

questions.title: Huntingdon Drive runs past number 10 — the record stops there
questions.detail: The record holds Huntingdon Drive as numbers 1 to 10. Dougal de Havilland's map draws a second run on the north-east side, numbered up the other way: 11 Burnham House, 13 The Magpies, 14 The Cottage, 15 The Coach House, The Hunting Lodge, 17, and 18 The Round House, formerly The Spiral, with Birchwood beyond. Only The Cottage is in the record, and only because a census household carried its name. Are these separate houses with their own numbers, or flats and coach houses belonging to houses already held? If they are houses, the record is missing half a street.

questions.title: Which of the two buildings by the tunnel is Gees Lodge?
questions.detail: Albert Drinkwater, a police constable, lived at "Gees Lodge, Tunnel Rd" in 1921 with his wife Ada and their son Harold. Two small buildings stand between Penrhyn House's garden and the road at the mouth of the Park Tunnel: the northern is still called Penrhyn Cottage, the southern is now called Tunnel Lodge. Gees Lodge is recorded on the southern one, since a lodge on Tunnel Road by the tunnel is the likelier of the two, but that is a judgement and not evidence. Is either still known by the older name? And is the reading Gees at all — the hand is loose enough that Cees or Lees are possible.

questions.title: Does anything of Barrack Yard survive, and exactly where was it?
questions.detail:
Three households were returned at "Barrack Yard, Barrack Lane" in 1911 — twelve people, all filed at 10 Barrack Lane because the enumerator counted the yard on the Barrack Lane round. Elizabeth Baker, a widow of 81, with her daughter and cabinet-maker son-in-law; Joseph Blythe, a sexton, with his wife, three children and a boarder; and Fletcher Hind, a domestic coachman, with his wife, a lace hand drawer, and their daughter, a hosiery machinist. A working court, in a lane otherwise recorded as eighteen numbered cottages.

It is now in the record as #410, placed at the foot of the lane just beyond number 30 and set back off the frontage. That position is worked out from Barrack Lane's own numbering and is provisional. Dougal de Havilland's map carries a note reading "Allegedly known as Barrack Yard" at the same end, around Pelham Cottages and Reveille, by the pedestrian access to Harlaxton Drive — allegedly is his word, and the map is far too coarse to place anything from.

Is the name still known? Does the entry or any of the cottages survive? And is the yard the block Dougal was pointing at, or somewhere else at that end of the lane?

questions.title: Is Yorke Mews its own address, or part of Yorke House?
questions.detail: A walk of the crescent turned up Yorke Mews, with the thought that it belongs to North Road rather than Cavendish Crescent North — made from an extension of the big house on the corner. The map agrees: Dougal de Havilland draws "Yorke Mews — The Lodge" and "formerly Yorke Cottage" immediately beside Yorke House, 6 North Road (#229), with The Coach House just beyond. So it is a mews of Yorke House. What is not known is whether it was ever a separate address with people returned at it, which is what it would take to give it a record of its own. Yorke Cottage is the older name and may be the one to search.

questions.title: 18 Cavendish Crescent North is still missing from the record
questions.detail:
The record held 16a and 18a but neither 16 nor 18 — although the listed-building descriptions of all four houses in that group name **"Nos. 16, 18, 20 and 22/24"** outright. They were built c.1885 as four substantial houses adjacent to each other, and three were later subdivided: the main part kept as one household, the former kitchen and butler's quarters made into a flat. So 16a is the flat of 16, and 18a the flat of 18.

**16 is now in the record as Crescent Lodge (#411)**, created because a census household was returned there. **18 still is not**, because nothing has yet been found living at it. What was 18 called, and is anyone on a return recorded there? And do 16 and 16a front the road differently, which would settle where each should sit on the map?

questions.title: 8 Cavendish Crescent North — the number survives on a door
questions.detail: The record runs 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 on the odd side and 10, 12, 14 upward on the even, with no 8 and no 6. A walk of the crescent found no house numbered 8, but **an old door with 8 on it at the back of the house below**. So the number was in use and the house has since been absorbed, renumbered or demolished. Which house does that door belong to now, and was 8 a separate dwelling?

questions.title: Western House School — sixty-three years, and two nights of it recorded
questions.detail:
**Where it was is settled, and it was in two places.** A. Hagues gives the school's span as **1873 to 1937**, founded by **Miss Louisa Clark on Western Terrace in 1874** and moved in **March 1890** to its final home at **30 The Ropewalk (#327)**. That resolves what looked like a contradiction between two returns: the **1881 census** heads the household 'Western Terrace (Western House), Boarding School' - Louisa Clark, 49, Principal of School, with the governess Isabella Huddleston, the teachers Ellen A. Hartt and Georgeana Barnblem, the pupil teachers Alice A. Eminson and Anna Toepken of Oldenburg, scholars, a cook and a housemaid - while the **1891 census** names it '30 Ropewalk (Western House)'. The school did not move between the two addresses by an enumerator's error; it moved by removal, a year before the later return. So Western Terrace was its home for sixteen years and The Ropewalk for forty-seven. The 1891 census names it outright — schedule 195, "30 Ropewalk (Western House)" — with Louisa Clark, 59, Principal of a Private School, and three resident governesses.

By **1911** the house holds twenty people and is run by **Annie and Florence Green**, sisters from Beverley, both returned as Principal, with six teachers, four servants and eight boarding pupils. The 1911 return does not give the school a name, so whether it was still called Western House under the Greens is unknown.

What is open: who ran it between Louisa Clark and the Greens, and after them to 1937; whether the name changed; and what became of the building. Directories and prospectuses would answer all three. **The Bangkok girls are accounted for.** Their father was almost certainly James Murchie (1865–1929), an engineer who went out to Singapore in 1891 and was sent on to Bangkok by Howarth Erskine Ltd, structural engineers in iron and steel, as their representative and general manager over a works of some six hundred men; he later joined the board, and by 1912 was trading in London as James Murchie & Co. Ltd. Doris Mary and Phyllis Kathleen were born at Bangkok in 1901 and 1903, with Janet Martha born at Much Wenlock in 1899 between them — a wife coming home for one confinement, and daughters later boarded in Nottingham while the family was abroad. The identification is inference and is recorded as such: no return or certificate here names him as their father, and the case rests on the place and the years agreeing. From the Stapleford and District Local History Society. What remains open about the school itself is unchanged: who ran it between Louisa Clark and the Greens, and after them to 1937; whether the name changed; and what became of the building.

questions.title: The Stables, Lenton Road — which house's stables?
questions.detail:
No census record in the record carries the address, so this comes from outside it. Two Lenton Road houses have a stables or coach house at the bottom of the garden, and both of those gardens back onto Clifton Terrace — the Gartree Lodge arrangement, where the outbuilding takes its address from the road behind.

**21 Lenton Road (#190)** is the stronger: its own listed description reads "Former coach house / stables building at bottom of garden facing Clifton Terrace now separately owned and converted for residential use" — separately owned is what gives a building its own address. **17 Lenton Road, Oakhyrst (#188)** has "Coach house and small outbuilding, now semi-derelict, added in garden area adjacent to Clifton Terrace c1900-1914". Cliff House (#196) has two flats in its converted coach house, but that is a 1959 conversion.

Dougal de Havilland's map carries three stables labels — "The Stables" beside The Chestnuts and 1 Kenilworth Road, and "The Stables 2a" with "Park Stables" over by Parkside and Lenton Avenue — but none of them on Lenton Road, so they are probably other buildings entirely.

Which house did it belong to, is it addressed on Lenton Road or Clifton Terrace, and was anyone ever returned as living there? 15, 17, 25 and 31 Lenton Road all hold people in 1911 and nobody at all in 1921, so there is room in the record for a household that has been filed somewhere else.

questions.title: The Bayley Hospital was at Lenton Abbey, outside The Park — and Newcastle Court took wounded
questions.detail:
**Both halves now answered.**

**Newcastle Court did take wounded.** Claire Birkin (#65) turned her own house, **Newcastle Court, Newcastle Circus (#207)**, into an auxiliary hospital for officers during the First World War. She was awarded the Médaille de la Reconnaissance Française and the Médaille de la Reine Élisabeth of Belgium for that work, and she was also Commandant of the Radcliffe on Trent VAD, president of the Belgian Red Cross committee in Nottingham and chair of the American Red Cross Society. From the Birkin family account, by A. Hagues.

**And the Bayley Hospital was not in The Park.** A. Hagues has placed it: it stood in the grounds of **Lenton Abbey**, off the south side of Derby Road (the A52) at NG9 2SN — west of Lenton, beyond this record's boundary. So the answer to the question as it was put is no: the Bayley Hospital is not one of ours, and none of the Derby Road numbers this record holds (117 to 173, and Rocky Mount) is the building. **Lilian Birkin** was its Matron and Commandant from October 1914; it was one of the first three auxiliary hospitals in England accepted by the War Office, took the first Belgian wounded from Antwerp on 21 October 1914, and more than 1,600 casualties over four years.

A. Hagues cites Historic England list entry 1247537 for Lenton Abbey alongside a sale listing. That entry is not in this record's own copy of the National Heritage List, which holds only the 101 entries inside The Park — correctly, since Lenton Abbey is outside it — and Historic England's site refuses automated requests, so the listing has not been read here. It is recorded on his authority rather than checked.

**What is still open**, and worth pulling: how Lilian and Claire Birkin were related, and whether any Park house besides Newcastle Court took patients. The name Bayley points at the family this record holds at 9 Cavendish Crescent — Thomas Bayley (#1) and his household — and whether they endowed or lent the hospital that carries their name is not known here. The British Red Cross VAD records are searchable and would answer the last of these.

questions.title: Kentmere: answered, it is on Pelham Crescent, not Cavendish Crescent North
questions.detail:
In 1911 William Wing, a solicitor of 47, lived at 'Kentmere, Cavendish Crescent North' with his wife Sara, his sons Henry, an automobile engineer, and Richard, an articled clerk, a cook and a housemaid. The four Wings are in the record (#668, #669, #670, #671) with that census and **no property**, and they stay unfiled by A. Hagues's decision until the house is identified. The name is on neither OpenStreetMap nor Dougal de Havilland's map.

**The directory confirms the name and the street, but gives no number.** Wright's Directory prints 'Kentmere, Wing William, solicitor (H. Wing & Son)' on Cavendish Crescent North in 1910-11 and 1913-14, 'Kentmere, Wing Henry' in 1913-14, and 'Kentmere, Wing Mrs. Sarah W' in 1915-16. So the house was called Kentmere for at least six years, and the family held it after William. Every one of those lines is printed without a number, as this crescent's named houses usually are.

**The firm ties the family to Park Terrace.** H. Wing & Son is the practice of Henry Wing, magistrate and solicitor, who is at 12 Park Terrace on the 1891 return with his daughter, his married granddaughter, her infant son, his sister-in-law and two servants, and whom Wright's prints at that number in 1894-95 and 1898-99. William, born about 1864, is the son of the firm's name.

**Correction: the earlier answer here was wrong.** This question used to reason that Kentmere was most likely number 1, now Carisbrooke House, 'which holds nobody in 1911'. It does hold a household in 1911: William Bradshaw and four others are filed at #21 that year. Since the enumerator reached the Wings *before* Bradshaw, Kentmere sits ahead of number 1 in the walk, at the North Road end, and cannot be number 1 itself.

**What is actually empty on the crescent in 1911**, for whoever picks this up: numbers 9 (#25), 10 (#26), 16a (#31) and 17 (#32). All four sit further along the crescent than the walk allows, so on present evidence Kentmere is a house the record does not hold at all, rather than one of these. Names on this crescent did change - 10 was formerly Charnwood - so a renaming is possible. A rate book, a deed, or the 1901 return for the same stretch would settle it.

**Answered by the 1901 return, which is what this question asked for.** Schedule 196 of the 1901 census reads **"Pelham Crescent, 'Kentmere'"** and gives William Wing, solicitor, 37, an employer, born in Nottinghamshire, with his wife Sarah W, 37, born at Sedgley in Staffordshire, his sons Henry, 11, and Richard, 8, and two servants, Maud Randeris and Kate Lansdall.

That is the same household the 1911 return puts at 'Kentmere, Cavendish Crescent North', ten years on and with the boys grown into an automobile engineer and an articled clerk.

**So the house is on Pelham Crescent.** The two crescents run into one another, and a corner house addressed both ways is a far smaller thing than a family moving and carrying the name with them. The reasoning above about which Cavendish Crescent North house could be Kentmere is therefore beside the point, and the four Wings (#668, #669, #670, #671) should be filed on Pelham Crescent once the number is known. The 1901 enumerator reached Kentmere at schedule 196, between "Carisbrooke Ho" at 195 and Julia Meyer's household at 197, which on the 1891 walk is the 1 Pelham Crescent end.

questions.title: Park Lodge is the last unplaced name on Tattershall Drive
questions.detail: Two of the three are settled. Belwood is the house at the corner with Tennis Drive, which carries the name on its door post and shares NG7 1AD with Ellington and the four flats at Tennis View; Ellington is Ellington House (#312), as expected. The Lodge is Gartree Lodge, 17a Tattershall Drive (#404), which is not what this question first guessed — it supposed The Lodge was the lodge beside the tennis ground that OpenStreetMap calls Park Lodge. That leaves Park Lodge itself, which the Land Registry holds separately at NG7 1BX alongside The Lodge, still unplaced. From HM Land Registry's price paid data, which records a house name beside the number for every sale since 1995. These are the names in use now, or recently — they may not be the historic ones, and a house name here is a lead, not a record. Under the rule for this record, none becomes a property until a census household is found at it, and Tattershall Drive holds no census household at all.

questions.title: Who ran Broadgate School after Ada Churley, and what happened to the houses in 1997?
questions.detail: Broadgate School occupied 1 and 2 Western Terrace from 1921 until 4 March 1997, initially run by Miss Ada Churley, who is on the 1921 census at number 1 as the principal of a school. Seventy-six years is longer than any household the record holds, and almost all of it is blank here: who ran the school after her, how many children it took, whether it used both houses from the start, and what became of the buildings after it closed. Both are flats now. Anyone who was taught there, or taught there, would settle most of this in an afternoon.

questions.title: Two girls' schools at 7 Western Terrace — when was each of them there?
questions.detail:
The house held Thornleigh Boarding and Day School for Girls, run by Miss E Leigh about 1900, and Auckland House School, a private boarding and day school for girls, briefly. Neither is dated here, and the record's only household at number 7 is the Hopewells in 1921 — a traveller of 65, his wife, a niece and two boarders — so neither school was there that year.

The 1901 return for the house should show Miss Leigh and her boarders outright, which would date Thornleigh and give the record a house full of women and girls that it does not have. Whether Auckland House came before or after is open, as is where each school went next. No Leigh is in the record at all.

Western Terrace held a third school in the same era: Broadgate took 1 and 2 from 1921 until 1997.

questions.title: Where is Claremont, and can the 1901 census place the Birkins in it?
questions.detail:
The Birkin family account puts Philip Austin Birkin at **Claremont** by the 1901 census. The record holds no house of that name, under any street or former name, and Philip appears in it only in 1911, at 5 Cavendish Crescent North — the house the account calls Blanbyre and the record holds as Blantyre House — where he is returned as a brewery manager.

So either Claremont is a Park house under a name this record does not yet know, or it stands outside the estate. The 1901 return that names it would settle both, and would be the evidence needed before any new property is created: nothing is added here without census data for it.

The same account places his brothers around him — Major Harry Birkin at Lincoln House on Lincoln Circus, Charles Wilfred at The Elms, now Newcastle Court, on Newcastle Circus, and Richard Lesley at Edale House on Clumber Road East. The record holds all three houses; Lincoln House has nobody in it at all.

**Overtaken in part: the record now holds a Claremont.** This question was written when no house of that name was in the record. **#230, 7 North Road**, built 1872, now carries Claremont as both its name and its former name, and the map labels it. So the question is no longer whether a Park house of that name exists, but whether *this* is the house the Birkin family account means, and whether the 1901 return puts Philip Austin Birkin in it. The 1901 household at #230 is William Smith, lace manufacturer, 79, his daughter Emily and three servants - not a Birkin - so either the account means a different house, or it means a different year. Claremont was briefly one of two candidates for Alfred William Stanfield's unnamed Lincoln Circus house. That is now superseded: his house is Lincoln House, on the circus itself. See [[stanfield-lincoln-circus-house]].

questions.title: Lincoln Circus 1 and 2 — which houses are they? The record holds only two on the circus
questions.detail:
**Settled: number 3 is Lincoln House.** Harry Laurence Birkin's household of eight — him at 49, a lace manufacturer, his wife Olive and six servants — is now filed there, on the strength of the family account that puts Major Harry Birkin opposite his brother.

**Settled: number 1 is Gladstone House.** The six returned at number 1 in 1921 are Alfred Charles Radford, 56, a lace and embroidery manufacturer, his wife Nellie, their daughter Doris, a trained nurse and two servants; Wright's Directory prints 'Gladstone house, Radford Alfd. Chas' on Lincoln Circus in 1910-11, 1913-14 and 1915-16. The Radfords' own 1911 household is now filed at Gladstone House.

**Number 2 is open.** Edward Palmer and his wife Alice are returned there in 1921, he as a gardener of 57. Ten years earlier the same two were filed at **Gladstone House**, where he gave the same trade. A. Hagues places the Palmers at The Cottage, Lincoln Circus, which the record does not yet hold; if The Cottage is number 2, a gardener's dwelling on the same ground, both returns agree and nothing needs a gardener living in the big house beside another family.

**Correction.** An earlier draft of this question named Annie Tune among Gladstone House's 1921 household. She is not there: the 1921 household is Wilfred Owen Woodward, his wife Vera Lilian, Harriet Elvina Weselby and Kathleen Edith Pollard. Annie Elizabeth Tune, cook, belongs to 1911 and to a different house — see [[stanfield-lincoln-circus-house]].

What is still wanted is a house for Stanfield, and a name for number 2.

**A cottage has been found in Lincoln House's grounds.** A. Hagues has identified a third building named The Cottage on the OS 1:1250 sheet of September 1953, on the Clumber Crescent North side of Lincoln House, which the record did not hold; it is now **#414**. The other two on that sheet were already held — #409, The Cottage, Tunnel Road, which belongs to Gladstone House, and #407, Penrhyn Cottage. The Palmers, returned at number 2 in 1921 and filed under Gladstone House in 1911, are very probably its household, which would make **The Cottage and 2 Lincoln Circus the same address** and close the number 2 part of this question. Its position is Lincoln House's own approximate one and wants fixing from the sheet.

**The circus is now fully accounted for in 1911.** The Palmers are filed at The Cottage (#414), Gladstone House holds the Radfords, and Lincoln House is answered as Alfred William Stanfield's - see [[stanfield-lincoln-circus-house]]. So every house on the circus has a 1911 household, which is what allowed Stanfield's to be settled by elimination. Whether The Cottage is also the number 2 of this question remains open: the Palmers are returned at 2 Lincoln Circus in 1921, and if that is the same dwelling then number 2 is answered too.

questions.title: 1 Duke William Mount has no census household at all — where are the Fishers?
questions.detail:
The house was built c1878-80 for Horace Arthur Fisher, who moved in with his wife Sarah Kate after their first child was born in 1883, and they had six children. Not one census record in this record is filed there — 1891, 1901 and 1911 should each show the family in the house, and 1921 whoever followed them.

Eight Fishers are now in the record from the family account, with names but almost no dates. Any return for the house would date the children, give their occupations, and name the servants who are certainly missing. Note that Horace the son went by Frank, so a page may read Frank Fisher.

questions.title: Arundel House stood from 1870 — why is Stephen Wills not in any census for it?
questions.detail:
T. C. Hine built the house in 1870 for the lace manufacturer Stephen Wills, and the record's only household there is 1921: George Edward Dixon, steward of an institute, with his wife, two daughters and a niece. Searching the census for Wills at the address has come up empty, which is worth thinking about rather than simply repeating.

Things worth trying. The house may not have been **numbered** in the early returns — enumerators often wrote the name alone, so look for *Arundel House, Park Valley* rather than number 1, and for the corner given as Lenton Road, since the house stands on the junction. The record does hold early returns nearby — 15 and 25 Park Valley, and 23 Lenton Road, reach back to 1871 and beyond — so the pages themselves exist and the house should be on them.

It is also worth allowing that **he never lived here**. A manufacturer could commission a house to let, or build it for a son or a daughter. A trade directory for the 1870s would place Stephen Wills at whatever address he actually occupied, and if that is somewhere else, the account's "built for" means built to his order, not lived in by him. The 1871 return, taken within a year of completion, is the one to find first.

questions.title: Are the three Brownsword households one family — and does Helena connect to them?
questions.detail:
The record now holds Brownswords in three places and does not say how, or whether, they join up. **John Hind Brownsword** (b.1836) with Mary, Edith Mary and John Anthony at #206, on the 1881 and 1891 returns. **Harry A. Brownsword** (b.1863), a lace manufacturer and an employer, with Mabel and their children Daphne, Norah and Douglas at 15 Lenton Road (#187) on the 1901 return, which came in this morning. And **Arthur Brownsword** (b.1870) at #44 and #206, who is already recorded as a cousin of Helena Brownsword Dowson (#2548).

Helena is the reason this matters. She was a leading Nottingham suffragist, a city councillor and a magistrate, and she has a Wikipedia article; her father was **Alderman Anderson Brownsword**, a Unitarian aligned with the Nottingham Liberal party, who is not in this record at all. Arthur and Harry were born seven years apart and both in Nottingham, and Brownsword is not a common name here. Nothing yet shows the tie, and none should be recorded until something does — a census, a will, a birth registration. Adding Anderson Brownsword himself would likely be the way in.

**A fourth Brownsword household, from the same 1901 round.** At schedule 184, a house called "St John's", **Mary Brownsword**, a widow of 65 born at Melbourne in Derbyshire, keeps house with her son **Arthur Brownsword**, 31, a lace manufacturer and an employer, born in Nottingham, and four servants.

Arthur born about 1870 in Nottingham is the Arthur already in the record at #44 and #206, recorded as a cousin of Helena Brownsword Dowson. **So this gives his mother, and she is a widow by 1901.** If Anderson Brownsword - Helena's father, the alderman who is not in this record at all - died before 1901, Mary is a candidate for his widow, and that would be the tie the question has been waiting for. A death registration for Anderson Brownsword, or Mary's own, would settle it.

questions.title: Henry Handford of Hardwicke House — which of Lord Belper’s daughters did he marry?
questions.detail:
**Answered, and he was.** Munk's Roll — the Royal College of Physicians' lives of its fellows, the entry by G. H. Brown from his 1928 obituaries in the Lancet and the British Medical Journal — gives Henry Handford as the son of Dr Thomas Handford of Atherstone, which is exactly where the 1901 census says the man at Hardwicke House was born. He trained at Edinburgh, taking his M.B., C.M. in 1878 with high distinction, then Paris and Vienna; tutored at Queen's College, Birmingham; came to Nottingham as physician to the General Hospital until 1906, strongest in pathology and diseases of the heart; and then spent twenty years as **medical officer of health for the county**, retiring in 1926. F.R.C.P. 1899. A major in the sanitary branch of the R.A.M.C. in the Great War. He died on 24 June 1928.

**What is still open** is his wife. Munk's Roll says only that she was *a daughter of the first Lord Belper* — Edward Strutt, of the Derbyshire cotton family — without naming her. The record holds her as Mary E. Handford, born 1854 at St George's in London, and she brought three grown daughters to the house, Gertrude, Sybil and Dorothy **Gale**, all born at Bedale in the North Riding between 1874 and 1876. So she married a Gale first and was widowed or otherwise free by the time the Handford sons arrived in 1894 and 1896. Which Strutt daughter she was, and who Gale was, neither the census nor Munk's Roll says. Burke's or the Strutt family papers would.

One discrepancy worth knowing: Munk's Roll dates his birth to **1855**, the record holds **1856** from his age on census night, and the second is the sort of year that is a year out as often as not.

**The sons.** Both were killed on the same morning. Captain Henry Basil Strutt Handford and Lieutenant Everard Francis Sale Handford, the boys of seven and five on the 1901 return, served together in the 1/8th Sherwood Foresters and died in the attack on the Hohenzollern Redoubt on 15 October 1915, aged twenty-one and twenty. Neither body was recovered; they are on the Loos Memorial, and a window in Southwell Minster remembers them together. Their brother-in-law Major John Pickard Becher D.S.O., husband of Gertrude Gale, was mortally wounded in the same attack and died on 1 January 1916. By then the family had left The Park for Elmfield at Southwell.

**One correction worth recording.** An account of the brothers gives their mother as a daughter of *Henry* Strutt, first Baron Belper. The barony was created in 1856 for **Edward** Strutt, and Henry was his son and the second baron — born 1840, fourteen years before Mary, so he cannot have been her father. Munk's Roll says simply "a daughter of the first Lord Belper", and that is what the record follows. Which daughter, and who the Gale was she married first, are still the open questions.

questions.title: The McCraiths at 7 Clumber Road: answered, it is 3 South Road
questions.detail:
Settled by A. Hagues from the census image. The record files the McCraith household at **3 South Road, Ellenborough House (#302)** for 1891, and the enumerator's page heads that same household **7 Clumber Road**. They are not two properties: the wife, both boys, the three-month-old Kenneth York and all four servants — Isabella Richardson, Elizabeth Smith, Lucy Else and Mary Jane Atkins — agree name for name with what the record already held.

So the house stays 3 South Road, and **7 Clumber Road is kept on it as a former address**, where it is searchable alongside Ellenborough House.

The page's *Jameston McCraith* is answered too: it is the enumerator running **James Wm** together, not a different forename. Two other hands on the same page were settled by the record rather than by reading — the page's *Hannett York* is **Kenneth York McCraith, b.1891**, and *Lucy Elso* is **Lucy Else, b.1869**, both already held at this house for 1891.

Still open, and not covered by this answer: the other numbered Clumber Road addresses on these pages — 3, 4, 5, 9 and 32 — which the record holds at no number at all.

questions.title: Clumber House on Clumber Road: answered, 15 Clumber Road is a former name
questions.detail:
Settled by A. Hagues from the census image. The record holds **Clumber House on Park Drive (#239)**, built about 1870–75. The 1891 census heads the Gregory household there twice as Clumber Road — once plainly, and once on a second page as **15 Clumber Road** with *"Clumber House"* written beneath it. Same family both times: William Godfrey Gregory, a lace manufacturer of 57, his wife Harriett, William, Ellen Augusta, Charles Arthur and Kate.

The house keeps Park Drive, and **15 Clumber Road is recorded on it as a former name**. The house has more than one frontage — its own description notes the original coach house was reached from Cavendish Crescent South — so an enumerator walking the Clumber Road round would address it that way.

This does not settle the other numbered Clumber Road entries on these pages. The record holds Clumber Road East, Clumber Road West and Clumber Crescent, every one of them by house name or Crescent number, and no numbered Clumber Road anywhere. Whether that numbering was a wider convention the estate later dropped is still worth knowing.

questions.title: Lynam or Lynum at Newcastle Court in 1891?
questions.detail:
The record holds the widow **Elizabeth Lynam (#52)** at Newcastle Court, Newcastle Circus (#207) for 1891, with her daughters Amelia Ann (#54), Helena Gertrude (#57) and Mabel Winifred (#58), and the servants Eliza Thorne (#62) and Emma Louise Skeggs (#63).

The 1891 enumerator's page heads that household *Newcastle Circus "THE ELMS"* — which is right, since #207 carries The Elms as a former name — and the surname there was transcribed **Lynum**, with a u. Same household either way: the daughters, both servants and the widow's age all agree.

So this is only about the spelling. Is the family Lynam or Lynum, and is the page's hand clear enough to settle it? The record's spelling should win unless the page plainly says otherwise, and if the page does say Lynum it is worth keeping as an alias so either spelling finds them.

questions.title: Two dates on the estate history where the map and the archive disagree
questions.detail:
The estate history now follows the University of Nottingham's archive wherever it disagrees with Dougal de Havilland's Park Map, on A. Hagues's instruction — they hold the Newcastle family papers. Six dates changed that way, and each entry keeps the map's own date beside it. Four are straightforward. **Two are not.**

**The castle, 1087.** The archive's timeline begins the first castle in 1087. The map says 1068 and credits William the Conqueror, ordering it raised by his son Peverel. The difficulty is that William died in September 1087, and 1068 — after the northern campaign — is the date usually given. 1087 may be the archive's own slip, or may refer to something later than the first earthwork. Worth checking against the printed timeline or the Newcastle papers themselves.

**The sale to Oxford, 1939.** The archive dates the 8th Duke's sale to Oxford University 1939. Both the map *and* the Nottingham Park Estate's own published history say **1938** — so here the archive stands alone against two sources, one of them the estate's own account of itself. This is the one correction where following the archive may be the wrong call.

The other four, for completeness: Cavendish's purchase of the ruin 1663 not 1662; the first house — St Mary's vicarage — 1809 not 1810; forty to fifty houses built by 1832 rather than fifty by 1834; and T. C. Hine appointed surveyor in 1854, not 1851 where the map places it alongside the 4th Duke's death.

questions.title: James Holroyd, house agent: 18 or 20 Barrack Lane?
questions.detail:
The 1911 return heads the Holroyd household **Harlaxton House, 18 Barrack Lane**, and that is where it is filed (#11). Wright's Directory of Nottingham puts him next door, three times over: 1910-11, 1913-14 and 1915-16 each print **"20 Holroyd James, house agent"**, always after Glenroy (F. W. Pare, no number given) and before 28 Simpson. See [1913-14, page 14](https://specialcollections.le.ac.uk/digital/collection/p16445coll4/id/166408), [1910-11](https://specialcollections.le.ac.uk/digital/collection/p16445coll4/id/165758) and [1915-16](https://specialcollections.le.ac.uk/digital/collection/p16445coll4/id/347693).

Neither 18 nor 20 has any other household in the record, so nothing here decides it. Either the enumerator's number or the directory's is wrong, or the lane was renumbered between the return and the directories' canvass. What would settle it: the 1921 return or the 1939 Register for either house, a rate book, or a deed naming Harlaxton House. If it turns out to be 20, move the household with the reassign page and add Harlaxton House as the house name there; if 18, add the house name to #11.

Glenroy is worth placing too: it sits between 10 and 20 in every directory, so it is likely one of 12 to 18.

questions.title: Where was William Henry Radford, engineer, in 1901?
questions.detail:
The record files **William Henry Radford (#3200)**, engineer to a lace manufacturer, as head at **Gleadthorpe, 11 Cavendish Crescent North** in 1901, with no age, from the note "engineer 1899 Wright's / lace manu 1901 census". A. Hagues now places the **McConnell** household at Gleadthorpe in 1901, and Wright's Directory agrees with him for 1894-95: "Gleadthorpe, Jno. M'Connell, warehouse manager" ([page 44](https://specialcollections.le.ac.uk/digital/collection/p16445coll4/id/164550)). The same page prints **Wm. Hy. Radford, engineer**, on the line after Gleadthorpe and before Flixton, as a separate entry with no house name, and 1898-99 starts its page with him in the same place ([page 50](https://specialcollections.le.ac.uk/digital/collection/p16445coll4/id/165226)). So he is next door to Gleadthorpe, not in it.

Which house is between Gleadthorpe (11) and Flixton (15): 12 Hazlewood or 14 Park House? Hazlewood is Thomas Page's in the directories, so **14 Park House (#29)** is the likeliest, but only the 1901 return for Radford can say. Once it is known, move #3200's 1901 record there with the reassign page.

He is not the coachman William Hy Radford of the Meyer household on Pelham Crescent in 1901, who is the William Edward Radford at 1 Pelham Crescent in 1911.

**Checked against the 1901 round now transcribed, and it does not answer this.** The pages read cover Cavendish Crescent North at schedules 189 to 195 - Hardwicke House, Haddon House, Peveril House (empty), one unnamed household under Donley Scott Ransom, Blantyre (empty), Cavendish Lodge and Carisbrooke House. **The numbered middle of the crescent, 11 to 15, is not among them**, so Gleadthorpe, Hazlewood, Park House and Flixton are all absent, and so is McConnell.

The only Radford anywhere in the transcribed 1901 rounds is **Wm. Hy. Radford, coachman, 40, born at Colston in Leicestershire**, in Julia Meyer's household at schedule 197 on Pelham Crescent - the very man this question already sets aside as the wrong Radford. So the question stands exactly where it did, and the page that would settle it has still to be read.

questions.title: Stanfield's house on Lincoln Circus: answered, it is Lincoln House
questions.detail:
**Answered by A. Hagues: Lincoln House (#403).** Alfred William Stanfield (#3554) is now a resident of it. The case is elimination rather than a document, so the whole of it is set out here.

**What was known.** Wright's Directory prints him on Lincoln Circus in 1910-11, 1913-14 and 1915-16, every time without a house name or number, and his obituary gives only 'his residence, Lincoln Circus, The Park'. He died there on 25 September 1918, a barrister and J.P. of 82 keeping three living-in servants.

**What closes it.** The circus holds three properties, and in 1911 two of them were full: Gladstone House had the Radfords, and The Cottage - identified only this week from the 1953 OS sheet - had the Palmers. **Lincoln House was the only empty house on Lincoln Circus that year**, in the very year his servants were returned at an unnamed house on it, with the cook Annie Elizabeth Tune signing the schedule for her absent master. He is also the only Lincoln Circus resident the 1910-11 directory prints with no house against his name.

**Nothing contradicts it.** Harry Laurence Birkin's household of eight is at Lincoln House on the 1921 return, three years after Stanfield's death, so the two do not overlap. Annie Elizabeth Tune is cook at 8 Western Terrace with the Bradleys by 1921 - a servant moving on when the household she kept was broken up by its master's death, which is what the dates require.

**What it rests on, and what would overturn it.** No schedule names Lincoln House as his address. If the 1911 enumerator's round for the circus is ever read and puts his three servants at another house, the resident link is the thing to undo. Two earlier candidates are superseded: Claremont (#230) and 1 Duke William Mount (#106) were suggested because both stood empty in 1911, but neither is on Lincoln Circus and neither was needed once the circus itself was found to have a vacancy.

**Still outstanding:** the three servants - Annie Elizabeth Tune (#595), Alice Ada Wright (#596) and Florence Swaly (#597) - have 1911 census rows still unfiled under 'Lincoln Circus (house not named)', and want reassigning to #403. Lincoln House is demolished and its position in the record is approximate.

questions.title: Which South Road house is Lindo House?
questions.detail:
The 1891 return puts Julius Meyer, commission merchant, born in Germany, with his wife Alice Ann, five children, a governess and three servants — eleven people — at **Lindo House, South Road**. The return gives no number, and no house of that name is in the record: a search of all 413 properties finds no Lindo at all. The nearest name, Linden House (#87, formerly The Lindens), is on Clumber Road West, a different street, and is already entangled with the Homberger filing. So the household sits unfiled under the address the return gives.

**What the directory adds, and what it does not.** Wright's Directory prints 'Julius Meyrick, of M. Schilling & Co.' on South Road in 1894-95 (page 136, Leicester Special Collections id 164642) and 1898-99 (page 146, id 165322), with no number and no house name, almost certainly the same man under an anglicised spelling. He is printed between Gardenhurst and Parkhurst. That does not yield a number, because the printed walk is not a numeric run: the 1894-95 order is Thorpe, Ellenborough House (3), Gardenhurst (5), Meyrick, Parkhurst (4), Evans. It places him between those two houses on the ground, nothing more.

**The candidates.** South Road holds six houses in the record, numbered 1 to 6 with no gap. In 1891 only number 2 (the Evanses) and number 3 (the McCraiths, Ellenborough House) hold anybody, so **1, 4, 5 and 6 are all empty that year**. Four candidates is too many to choose from on position alone, and filing eleven people on a guess would be costly to unpick.

**What would settle it** is the 1891 enumerator's walk. The census route is geographic, so the schedules either side of Lindo House on the page — particularly its distance from Ellenborough House or from the Evanses at number 2 — would give the position directly. A. Hagues has transcribed the Evans household from that street and year, so the page may already be to hand.

**A loose end found alongside it, now settled:** the record dated Parkhurst, 4 South Road (#303), to 1925, against a directory that prints the house in 1894-95. A. Hagues has corrected the date to 1870. See [[parkhurst-build-date]].

**Being asked on the ground.** A. Hagues is putting the question to the current owners, which is the kind of answer this cannot be reasoned into. Meanwhile the candidates have narrowed: filing the Thorpe household at 1 South Road leaves the street's 1891 occupancy as 1 Thorpe, 2 Evans, 3 McCraith, so only 4, 5 and 6 stand empty. Of those, 4 is Parkhurst and 5 is Gardenhurst, both printed under their own names in the directory with other householders, which leaves **6 South Road** as the single unnamed vacancy. That is a narrowing and not a finding: the Thorpe case ended by showing that a house can sit on a corner and be addressed to another street entirely, so nothing is filed on it.

questions.title: Pelham Terrace and Newcastle Drive: how do the 1891 numbers convert?
questions.detail:
**Settled: the Newcastle Drive schedules mean Newcastle Drive.** The 1891 enumerator headed schedules 84 to 88 as 13, 11, 9, 7 and 5 Newcastle drive - Kidd, Taylor, Kentish Wright, Birkin and Hill - so those houses are filed on the numbers the return gives. For 1, 3, 5, 9 and 13 the 1894-95 directory independently names the same householder at the same number, and those five are the only numbers that volume prints for the street.

**Settled: the street's history.** Newcastle Drive was formerly two roads, Lower Newcastle Terrace and Pelham Terrace (A. Hagues). Seventeen listed-building descriptions already in the record say 'Newcastle Drive, formerly named Pelham Terrace', and 35 Newcastle Drive carries the name Pelham House. The road was cut below Newcastle Terrace as part of T. C. Hine's plan for the 5th Duke of Newcastle, halving the width of the terrace above to allow Italianate villas with terraced gardens below.

**The working rule: Newcastle Drive number = 39 minus the Pelham Terrace number.** Two independent confirmations:
- **12 Pelham Terrace = Glendower = 27 Newcastle Drive**, and this one is as firm as anything short of a deed. William Foster junior, cabinet maker and upholsterer, is at 12 Pelham Terrace on the 1891 return with his wife Mary, 45. The 1898-99 directory prints 'Glendower, William Foster, of Foster, Cooper & Foster' against the number 12. The 1913-14 and 1915-16 volumes print 'Foster William, (Foster, Cooper & Foster)' at 27 Newcastle Drive. The Park Houses map labels 27 Newcastle Drive **Glendower** (now subdivided as 27, 27B, 27C and 27D). And the record holds Mary Foster, born 1846, at 27 Newcastle Drive on the 1921 return. Same man, same wife, same house name, four sources. 39 - 12 = 27. Glendower appears nowhere in the record as a house name and is worth adding to #221.
- **24 Pelham Terrace = 15 Newcastle Drive**, from a published account of that house. 39 - 24 = 15.

**What the rule predicts for the rest of the 1891 walk**, which began at Tattershall Corner: 4 Pelham Terrace (Edmund Pratt, lace manufacturer) becomes 35, which is **Pelham House**, built 1860 - a named villa for a substantial household, which fits; 6 becomes 33 and was uninhabited; 8 (John Sylvester, baker) becomes 31; 10 (Job Samuel W. Palethorpe, engraver) becomes 29; 14 (John Jardine, lace machinery, of the firm behind Ernest Jardine) becomes 25; 16 (David Shaw Ramsay) becomes 23; and 18, **Wolsley House** (Samuel Maples, solicitor, notary and under-sheriff, of Maples & McCraith) becomes 21. Every one of those houses exists in the record with a build date before 1891. Wolsley House appears nowhere in the record, so that name is untested.

**Where the rule breaks, and why that may be the answer.** The same walk has 19 and 21 Pelham Terrace, and 39 - 19 = 20, an even number on a street numbered wholly in odds. Since Newcastle Drive was *two* former roads, the odd Pelham Terrace numbers may belong to the Lower Newcastle Terrace stretch, or to the opposite side. Until that is understood the rule converts the even numbers only.

**A heading error in the 1898-99 volume, now identified.** That volume prints an even-numbered 'Pelham Crescent' section - 2, 4, 6, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 20 - which includes Job S. Palethorpe at 10 and Glendower at 12, the very numbers and householders the 1891 census puts on Pelham **Terrace**. These are not crescent addresses. Pelham Crescent does have a real even side: 10 and 12 Pelham Crescent (#279, #281) are a pair of houses of about 1870-75, possibly by John Loverseed, facing the crescent with their basements at garden level on Barrack Lane, and the 1911 census has the Mellers at 10 and the Levis at 12. The later volumes list that side properly, with Mann, Shaw, Ling, Pinder and Pearson. So the 1898-99 compiler put a run of Pelham Terrace houses under a Pelham Crescent heading, and any use of that volume's even-numbered crescent lines has to be checked against the census before it is trusted. The odd-numbered crescent lines, 1 to 19, are unaffected.

**One caveat on the anchor.** The record's 39 Newcastle Drive is Priests House, whose former names include Tattershall Corner - where the 1891 walk starts, with Bernard Wilcockson, solicitor - but its build date is 1911, so the present house is not the one on the 1891 return. The name marks the corner rather than the building.

What would settle the whole street: a rate book, or the 1901 return, which should name the houses under whichever name was then current.

**Settled: the name changed before the numbers did, and the two ranges tile.** A published account of John Jardine (1825-1895) puts him on the 1881 census at **14 Newcastle drive** - the same house the 1891 enumerator heads 14 Pelham Terrace. The record holds no even numbers anywhere on Newcastle Drive, so an 1881 'number 14' cannot be a modern address; the street had taken the name Newcastle Drive by 1881 while the old Pelham Terrace numbers were still in use, and the renumbering came afterwards. That explains why one 1891 page carries both namings, and it makes the street account for itself: the lower end was enumerated in 1891 as Newcastle drive with the modern numbers 1 to 13, which is why those five match the 1894-95 directory; the upper end was still Pelham Terrace with its own numbers 4 to 19, which convert by 39 minus n into 21 to 35; the published 24 to 15 fills 20, 22 and 24 into 19, 17 and 15; and 37 and 39 are left for the corner at Tattershall. No number is claimed twice and none is left over.

questions.title: Parkhurst, 4 South Road: the 1925 build date was wrong, and is now 1870
questions.detail:
**Settled.** The record dated 4 South Road, also known as Parkhurst, to **1925**. Three things contradicted it, and A. Hagues has corrected the date to **1870**.

- **The property's own history text**, in the same record, reads 'One of a pair of houses (with 3 Clumber Crescent South). Possibly by architects Hine & Son **1870-75**.' The field and the prose beside it disagreed.
- **Its pair.** 5 South Road, Gardenhurst (#304), is dated **1870** and described in the same terms - one of a pair, possibly Hine & Son 1870-75. Two houses built together should not be dated fifty-five years apart.
- **The directory.** Wright's prints 'Parkhurst, Mrs. Sarah A. Gamble' on South Road in **1894-95** and **1898-99**, and 'Parkhurst, Walker Joseph' in 1910-11. People were living in the house three decades before 1925.

The 1925 figure may have come from a later alteration rather than nothing at all: the history notes the house is now converted into flats, and the description records an early twentieth-century lean-to and a later single-storey extension in the yard toward Clumber Crescent South. If a date for the conversion turns up, it belongs in the history text rather than in the build date. Kept here so that 1925 is not entered again from whatever source first supplied it.

questions.title: Which house was Newcastle House in 1891?
questions.detail:
Arthur Bee, butler, 48, with his wife Mary, his son Arthur Henry, a clerk in a lace warehouse, and his daughter Mary Corner Bee, a dressmaker, are returned at **Newcastle House** on the 1891 census. All four (#3490-#3493) are in the record **unfiled**, by A. Hagues's decision, because no property of that name exists and the evidence for placing them is all from a later date.

**What points at 19 Park Terrace.** Wright's Directory prints 'Newcastle house, Clark Wm. Froggatt, (Nottingham Mills Co)' on Park Terrace in 1910-11, 1913-14 and 1915-16, and the record has William Froggatt Clark as head of **19 Park Terrace** (#379) on both the 1911 and 1921 returns. Same man, same house name, same street: 19 Park Terrace was Newcastle House in the 1910s.

**Why that is not enough for 1891.** The gap is nineteen years, and a house name can move to a neighbouring building or a number be re-cut in that time. Worse for the inference, the directory shows Clark somewhere else earlier: 'Wm. F. Clark, of Nottm Mills Co.' is printed at **11 Park Terrace** in 1894-95 and 1898-99. So he reached Newcastle House between 1899 and 1910, and in 1891 the house was somebody else's - which is consistent with the Bees being there, but leaves the building unidentified.

**Two other things worth weighing.** #379 is a census-only property: no build date, no description, nothing but returns. And a butler as head of household, with his own grown children working outside the house and no employer's family on the schedule, usually means a lodge, a coach house or rooms over stables rather than the principal house - or a house being kept while its owners were away. Which it was changes what Newcastle House means on this return.

**What would settle it cheaply:** the 1891 enumerator's walk. If the Bees' schedule sits among the Park Terrace numbers near 19, the identification holds; if it sits elsewhere, it does not. The page is in A. Hagues's hands. Failing that, a rate book or the 1901 return for the same stretch would name the house.

questions.title: 13 Cavendish Crescent South is the house now numbered 1 South Road
questions.detail:
**Answered by A. Hagues.** Eight people are returned on the 1891 census at **13 Cavendish Crescent South** - Roby Eddington Thorpe (#3184), 51, solicitor and farmer; his wife Nelly (#3185), 46; their daughter Dorothea Mary Roby (#3186), 15; **Mary Mundella** (#3187), 58, visiting; and four servants, Ellen Savinge (#3188), Selina Draycott (#3189), Emma Bussenhart (#3190) and Grace Leech (#3191). No number 13 exists in the record or in any directory volume, so they were held unfiled. They are now filed at **1 South Road (#301)**, and 13 Cavendish Crescent South is kept on that property as a former address.

**The house has gates onto both roads.** The record's own description of #301 records 'original gate piers on Cavendish Crescent South and South Road', and a later extension and porch adjacent to Cavendish Crescent South. A corner house with two frontages can be addressed to either, which is the whole of the difficulty.

**The number survives on the outbuilding.** A. Hagues found a street view of the site: the sign reads **13, The Studio**, on a converted range beside a garage, attached to the main house. The record's description of #301 accounts for both - 'plan by H. Butler for garage building for James Curnow c1920' and 'outbuildings altered/rebuilt to form residential accommodation'. So 13 did not disappear; it stayed on the annexe when the principal house was re-addressed to South Road. The studio is a one-bedroom flat today and could never have held a household of eight, but in 1891 it was still an outbuilding, and 13 was the main house's number on its crescent frontage.

**The same thing happened next door.** Ellenborough House, 3 South Road (#302), was returned in 1891 as **7 Clumber Road**, and that is kept on it as a former address. Two houses at the same junction, in the same census, addressed to roads other than the ones they now belong to.

**Supporting, and worth keeping in view:** 1 South Road held no 1891 census at all while both its neighbours did - the Evanses at 2 and the McCraiths at 3 - so a corner house stood apparently empty in a year when an eight-person household nearby had nowhere to go.

**The one thing unchecked.** On the enumerator's south-side page the household falls between number 7 and number 15, where 9, 11 and 13 would be, rather than at the end of a run; 9 and 11 appear nowhere on that page. The schedule numbers either side of the Thorpes would confirm this reading or overturn it. Mary Mundella, visiting, may also connect this household to the Mundella on the lace makers' watch list, which is a separate thread worth pulling.

questions.title: Who built Glendower, 27 Newcastle Drive — and is the Fothergill attribution right?
questions.detail:
The record gives **27 Newcastle Drive** as 'Large detached house c1884, by Watson Fothergill architect', and its architect field says Watson Fothergill. A. Hagues doubts it, and has found something that points elsewhere.

**What the house is.** Glendower, built for **William Foster** of Foster, Cooper & Foster, the furnishing firm. Foster is at 12 Pelham Terrace on the 1891 census — the same house, before the street was renumbered — and the 1898-99 directory names it Glendower. The initials **WF** are inscribed on the front, which A. Hagues notes could as easily stand for the owner, William Foster, as for Watson Fothergill; the same two letters serving both men is exactly the sort of coincidence an attribution can be built on by mistake.

**What points at Bromley.** The Nottingham Journal of **10 November 1881** carries **Albert Nelson Bromley** tendering for builders to work on a furniture depository for Foster's company. So Bromley was working for this client, on this firm's buildings, three years before the house is dated. Bromley was born at Stafford in 1850 and the directory prints him at **15 Newcastle Drive** from 1898-99 through 1915-16 — a few doors from Glendower, on the same street. He is now on the architects' watch list.

**The record already knows his practice, but not the man.** Two property descriptions name later forms of the firm: 'Bromley, Cartwright and Waumsley' for alterations at 3 Cavendish Crescent North about 1933, and 'Bromley and Cartwright' for a flat conversion at 4 Western Terrace about 1948. Albert Nelson Bromley himself appears nowhere in the record — not as a person, not among the sixteen architects, not among the fourteen firms.

**Nothing has been changed.** The architect field still reads Watson Fothergill, because a tender for a different building by the same client is a lead and not an attribution. What would settle it: a drawing or a building notice for the house itself, a dated plan in the estate archives, or Fothergill's own job list, which is well documented and would either include Glendower or not. If it is not his, the field and the history note both want correcting, and Bromley wants adding as an architect in his own right.

questions.title: John Loverseed Mann: how are the Manns and the Loverseeds related?
questions.detail:
A probate notice in the Nottingham Weekly Press of 1 May 1908 gives the full name of the man the record holds as 'John L Mann' (#3306) of 5 North Road: **John Loverseed Mann**. A middle name of that kind is usually a mother's maiden name, and it is the first hard link between two families the record had only as neighbours.

**What the record holds of each.** The Manns: John Loverseed Mann, cardboard box manufacturer, late of Thomas Mann and Co. of Postern Place, died 16 March 1908 aged 44; his widow **Alice** carried the business on and is returned at 5 North Road in 1911 as a cardboard box manufacturer in her own right; their son Thomas is with her. Wright's Directory also prints 'Thomas Mann, box manufacturer' on Pelham Crescent in 1894-95 - presumably the firm's founder and very likely his father - and 'John L. Mann, of Mann & Son' on North Road the same year.

**The Loverseeds** are all over the same streets. Edwin Gauntley Loverseed held **2 Western Terrace** from 1894-95 to 1915-16 and is there on the 1911 return with his wife and three daughters. **Sarah Loverseed** had **1 Western Terrace** in 1894-95 and 1898-99, before the Patons. **A. W. Loverseed** was at Pelham Lodge on Pelham Crescent in 1894-95. And the record's own descriptions of **10 and 12 Pelham Crescent** call them 'one of a pair of houses c1870-75 possibly by John Loverseed' - so the name attaches to the building of the estate as well as to living on it.

**What would settle it:** John Loverseed Mann's birth or marriage registration, which would give his mother's maiden name outright, or Thomas Mann's marriage. If the mother was a Loverseed, it ties a box-manufacturing family to a building one across four houses, and may explain how the Manns came to be in The Park at all. Nothing is joined on the strength of a middle name alone.

**Also outstanding:** #3306 is recorded as 'John L Mann' and wants renaming to **John Loverseed Mann**, which an import cannot do.

**Advanced by the 1891 return: they were next-door neighbours.** The census puts **Thomas Mann, cardboard box manufacturer, at 14 Pelham Crescent** with his wife Mary Ann, his son **John Loverseed Mann, 27, a cashier**, his daughter Nellie Annie and a servant - and **Arthur Wellington Loverseed at 16 Pelham Crescent**, immediately adjacent, with his wife Kate, six children and their servant Esther Holland. So the two families were not merely on the same streets: they were side by side, and the Mann son carried the neighbour's surname as his middle name. Arthur Wellington Loverseed, returned as living on his own means, is very probably the 'A. W. Loverseed, Pelham lodge' the directory prints on the crescent in 1894-95. Thomas Mann is created from this page; he was not in the record at all, though the directory prints him as a box manufacturer on Pelham Crescent in 1894-95 and the firm his son died as part of was Thomas Mann and Co.

**It still does not prove the descent.** Mary Ann Mann's maiden name is not on the 1891 schedule, and nothing there says she was a Loverseed. Her marriage, or her son's birth registration, would give it outright. What the page removes is the possibility that the middle name was a coincidence.

**A duplicate found alongside it.** The record holds this man twice: **#3306 John Loverseed Mann**, with the probate biography and the 1908 death, and **#3689 John L Mann**, born 1864, same 1901 household, no biography. They are one person entered under a census short form. Keep #3306, which carries everything, and join them with **Join up people entered under a census short form** on the admin page.

questions.title: Peveril Drive: which house is Parkdale, which is Dudley Lodge, and where is Castle Rock?
questions.detail:
**Settled by A. Hagues, from the 1911 census key and his own knowledge of the street.** The 1911 return names six houses on Peveril Drive that the record held only partly, and two of them had been put on the wrong properties.

- **11 Peveril Drive (#296) is Ivanhoe Lodge** - 'I used to walk past it.' The record already had that as its house name, but also carried **Dudley Lodge** as a former name, taken from the OS 1:1250 sheet. That has been removed: Dudley Lodge is a different house, and the 1911 key lists Ivanhoe Lodge and Dudley Lodge as two separate households on the same page, so one property cannot be both.
- **12 Peveril Drive (#297) is Dudley Lodge.** The record had it as **Parkdale**, sourced to A. Hagues himself; he now corrects that. Parkdale is kept on #297 as a former name only because the record carried it until now - not because the house bore it.
- **Parkdale is #299**, the unnumbered property of that name, which he confirms. The census supports it independently: the household his key places at Park Dale - Woodward, Cole, Barker and Galpin - is already filed at #299 for 1911.
- **Castle Rock is 5 Peveril Drive (#376)**, now named. The modern map shows 1 and 2 Castle Rock beside The Coach House; he judges the census Castle Rock to be the one now numbered 2, number 1 not having existed then. This is the least corroborated of the four - no directory line or OS sheet has been checked against it yet.
- **7 Peveril Drive (#293)** already carries Harlech House as a former name, matching the key's Harlech.
- **Easdale** (the Polley household) has no property in the record and is not created here.

**Why this mattered.** Twenty-two people sat unfiled under a single label, 'PeD1 Peveril Drive', which was a load artefact rather than an address: the first household's tag had been applied to a whole page of five families. A. Hagues supplied the key that splits them, and the house names above are what allow most of them to be placed.

**The 1901 return has now been read, and it tests all of this.** The enumerator walked the drive giving house names and almost no numbers, exactly as 1911 does: Dudley Lodge, Harlech House, Homebush, Thorndale, Castle Rd House and Sunnyside, with only No 3 numbered - August R. von Renesse, a lace warehouse manager and a German subject, keeping house with his mother-in-law and two servants.

**Four of the six confirm the settlement above.** Dudley Lodge, Harlech House and Castle Rd House are the names now held at #297, #293 and (as Castle Rock) #376, and Ivanhoe stood **uninhabited** on census night 1901, which fits a house the record holds at #296. Park Dale, at schedule 228, is Fredk J. Elborough's household of eight and belongs to #299.

**Three names are new to this street, and two of them collide with houses elsewhere in The Park.** Homebush held Edward Sanderson, a widowed shipping and forwarding agent, with three grown children; **Thorndale** held Henry Towle, station master on the Midland Railway; **Sunnyside** held Herbert Norrell, a railway contractor of 29. Two railwaymen next door to one another is the kind of pattern a directory will confirm.

**Homebush has no property in the record at all.** But **Thorndale is carried as a former name of 24 Hamilton Drive (#125)**, and **Sunnyside is a property in its own right on Park Terrace (#390)**. Neither is on Peveril Drive. So either the name was used twice in The Park, or the 1901 enumerator's Peveril Drive round strayed into a neighbouring street, or one of the existing records has the street wrong.

**Thorndale is answered, and it is a corner house - which is why two sources appeared to disagree.** Wright's Directory prints **Henry Towle, M.R. station master, at Thorndale** under **Hamilton Drive** in 1894-95 and 1898-99, with Henry Vickers there from 1910-11. The OS 1:1250 sheet draws **Thorndale in the row with Parkdale, Dudley Lodge, Harlech House and Woodley**, which are Peveril Drive houses.

**Both are right.** The record's own account of #125 settles it: *a semi-detached house adjacent to 8 Peveril Drive, on a prominent corner plot at the junction of Hamilton Drive and Peveril Drive, one of a group also including 8, 10, 12 and Parkdale on Peveril Drive.* It is numbered on Hamilton Drive and built as part of the Peveril Drive terrace, so a directory files it under one street and a map draws it in the other's row.

**A correction to what was written here earlier today.** I recorded that the directory proved Thorndale to be a Hamilton Drive house and that my reading of the 1901 round - which had placed Henry Towle's household on Peveril Drive - was simply wrong. That was too strong. The 1901 enumerator gave the house name and no street, and a house on this corner can honestly be written up under either; the household belongs at **#125** whichever street heads the schedule.

**Sunnyside is still open.** No directory volume prints it, on Peveril Drive or anywhere else. The record holds a Sunnyside on Park Terrace (#390), and whether Herbert Norrell's household of 1901 belongs there, or at a Peveril Drive house of the same name, is unsettled. Nothing should be filed at #390 from this round until it is.

**Homebush is answered too**: the 1898-99 directory prints *Homebush, Jph. Adams, of S. Adams & Sons* on **Peveril Drive**, so the name does belong to this street even though the record holds no property of it. It wants creating before Edward Sanderson's household can be filed.

**Four more 1901 households on the drive carry neither name nor number** - Francis Budd the wine merchant, John C. Wright, Tom King and Albert Ley - and cannot be placed from this return at all.

**THE OS 1:1250 SHEET NAMES FOUR HOUSES THE RECORD DOES NOT HOLD.** Supplied by A. Hagues. Reading the block between Kenilworth Road and Peveril Drive, the sheet gives in order: **Parkdale, Dudley Lodge, Harleck House** (so spelt), **Woodley, Thorndale**. Woodley sits between Harlech House and Thorndale and is in no property record.

Along the north side of Hamilton Drive it gives **Easdale, Ferndene, Clovelly** and **The Limes**. Only Ferndene is held (#298). **Easdale** is the name this question already wanted: the Polley household of the 1911 key has nowhere to go, and here is the house on a map.

**Ferndene's neighbours explain themselves.** The record says #293 is the central section of a building holding *6, 7 and Ferndene*, and #298 says the same - so Harlech House at 7 Peveril Drive and Ferndene are parts of one structure, which is why the map draws them close together and why the numbering runs oddly.

**Still wanted:** a property for Woodley, Clovelly, The Limes and Easdale, and a date for the sheet, which looks like the 1950s revision and so records names a half-century after the censuses this record is built on.

questions.title: 5 Clumber Crescent South or Clumber Court - which held the Kippings in 1921, and which the McCraiths?
questions.detail:
**The crescent held five households in 1921 and three are settled.** Kirkaldy is at number 3 on the strength of Professor Adam Willis Kirkaldy's will, reported in the Nottingham Evening Post of 28 March 1932, which calls him formerly of 3 Clumber-crescent; the notice does not say north or south, but the north crescent holds only Cedar Lodge and no numbers at all, so the address can only be this one. Lewenz is at number 7, the single house number any of the five schedules gives. Jardine is at number 9, where the family is returned in 1901 and 1911, printed in Wright's Directory from 1910-11 to 1915-16, and still found on the 1939 register; Mary Evanson is cook there in both 1911 and 1921, which fixes that household to the house independently of the enumerator's walk.

**That leaves two houses and two households, and nothing separates them.** The houses are 5 Clumber Crescent South (#79) and Clumber Court (#399). The households are Frederick Stanley Kipping, professor of chemistry at University College, eleven people including the visiting Jinks family and his mother-in-law; and James William McCraith, eleven people including four McCraiths, two visitors and five servants.

**What has already been tried.** Wright's Directory prints two Perry households on the crescent without numbers in 1910-11, 1913-14 and 1915-16 - Mrs John Maddock Perry and John Thorpe Perry - and John Thorpe Perry is returned at number 5 in 1911, so the other Perry household is presumably at Clumber Court; but neither Perry connects to Kipping or to McCraith. Kipping, Kirkaldy, Lewenz and Wigglesworth appear in no volume of the directory at all, so that source is exhausted. The McCraiths come to the crescent from Ellenborough House, 3 South Road, where the record holds them from 1881 with their servant Isabella Richardson; nothing in that line names a house here. Two published lives of Kipping - F. Challenger's Royal Society obituary notice of 1950 and N. R. Thomas's paper in Silicon of 2010 - give his career in full and neither names his Park address. Thomas has him a regular at the Nottingham Park Tennis Club; Challenger places him at 40 Magdala Road, which is not on the estate and whose relation to the 1921 return is unknown.
