**Where both households sit now.** The McCraith household is eleven unfiled 1921 rows under the label Clumber Crescent South. The Kipping household was imported with its rows deliberately unfiled under the same label. Neither should be filed by interpolating the walk. See [[clumber-court-stub]].

**Where the Kippings were twenty years earlier, which is new ground for this question.** The 1901 census puts the household on **Clumber Road West** - Frederic Stanley Kipping, 37, professor of chemistry, his wife, two children born in Scotland and Middlesex, his mother-in-law Florence Holland, and two servants. A. Hagues reads the enumerator's round as Ernest Jardine, then 6 Clumber Road, then Hesse, then Felixstowe, and then this household, which places it at **Holly Lodge (#86)**, and it is filed there.

**This does not settle 1921**, and should not be made to. But it does two useful things. It shows the family held a house in The Park long before the return that is in dispute, so the 1921 household is a return to the estate rather than an arrival on it. And it puts **Ernest Jardine on the same 1901 round**, which matters because Jardine is the household already fixed to 9 Clumber Crescent South by his cook in two censuses - so the two families were neighbours of a sort in 1901 as well as in 1921.

**A caveat that belongs with it.** Schedules 150 to 179 are absent from the pages read, so the order of that round is A. Hagues's and cannot be checked against the transcription. If it is ever shown to run otherwise, Holly Lodge is the thing to undo.

questions.title: The Holland sisters and the Duvals - are the Bridgwater and Liverpool Hollands one family?
questions.detail:
**Three chemists married three sisters.** Frederic Stanley Kipping married Lily Holland at Bridgwater on 3 March 1888; William H. Perkin junior had married her elder sister Mina at the same church on New Year's Eve 1887; and Arthur Lapworth married Kathleen Holland at St Mary's, Bridgwater, on 14 September 1900. Their father was W. T. Holland, J.P., of Bridgwater in Somerset. Both published lives of Kipping - F. Challenger's Royal Society obituary notice of 1950 and N. R. Thomas's paper in Silicon of 2010 - add that the sisters were granddaughters of Charles Allen Duval, so their mother was a Duval who married a Holland.

**A second Duval-Holland marriage is recorded elsewhere.** Charles Allen Duval (1810-1872) was born at Beaumaris in Anglesey and settled in Manchester as a portrait painter and photographer. His Wikipedia article names a daughter Florence who married Dr Charles Thurstan Holland, the radiologist, of Liverpool - a different Holland from W. T. Holland of Bridgwater, and of a later generation, Thurstan Holland having been born in 1863. That article also lists at least one granddaughter among his children, so its account of the family is not wholly reliable and should not be built on unchecked.

**Why it matters to The Park.** The 1921 return for the Kipping household on Clumber Crescent South gives a mother-in-law, Florence Holland, 78, born in Manchester, which would make her the Duval daughter who married W. T. Holland. If she is, then the Bridgwater and Liverpool Hollands are either one family or two that each married a Duval, and the Kipping, Perkin and Lapworth marriages sit inside a much larger network. If she is not, the Manchester birthplace on that schedule wants another explanation.

**That caution is now spent - the two women are separated.** #1329 is the Kipping mother-in-law, born 1843 at Manchester. The maid of the same name at 23 Cavendish Crescent South is #3692, born 1882 at Nottingham. Nothing further need be untangled before working on this. Duval himself is not created: he died in 1872, eleven years before Kipping was born, and has no connection to the estate. See [[kipping-mccraith-which-house]].

**The 1901 census gives her a second time, and independently.** She is in the Kipping household on Clumber Road West that year as mother-in-law, a widow of 58, born at Manchester - so a birth year of 1843 twice over, twenty years apart, on two different schedules. The Manchester birthplace that the whole Duval argument rests on is therefore not a single clerk's entry that might be wrong, and she was already widowed by 1901, which dates W. T. Holland's death before that.

**A small thing that runs the same way.** The Kippings' housemaid in 1901, **Ellen M Norman**, sixteen, was born at **Bridgwater in Somerset** - the Hollands' own town, and the town where all three sisters were married. A servant of that age carrying that birthplace is likelier to have come to Nottingham with the family than to have been hired here, which is one more thread between this household and Bridgwater.

Duval himself is still not created, for the reason given above.

questions.title: Who were the two lace manufacturers at Carisbrooke House in 1891? The surname will not read
questions.detail:
**Schedule 8 of the 1891 census gives Carisbrooke House to two unmarried brothers**, the head 36 and his brother 34, both lace manufacturers and both born in Nottingham, with an aunt of 66 named Ann Ward and two general servants, Georgina Sharp and Eliza Turfitt. The household is straightforward. The surname is not.

**It has been set down as Pheeps, which is certainly wrong** - a placeholder standing in for a hand that will not resolve. It is written the same way twice, once for each brother, so it is not a slip of the enumerator's pen.

**What would settle it.** A Nottingham lace firm run by two brothers born about 1855 and 1857, unmarried and living together in The Park in 1891, should appear in Wright's Directory for 1891-92 or thereabouts. The aunt Ann Ward may be the easier thread: the record already holds a '? Ward' at 17 Cavendish Crescent North, a forename lost the same way, and the two may be the same woman.

questions.title: Cavendish Crescent North in 1881: the record holds nothing at all
questions.detail:
**Six households, about forty people, and not one of them in the record.** The 1881 enumerator's schedules 106 to 111 walk the crescent: Carisbrooke House under John G Woodward, Cavendish Lodge under Alfred Goater the printer employing three hundred hands, James B Walker the lace manufacturer, Thomas Bayley the leather merchant, Thomas Walker the seed crusher, and Hardwicke House under John W Lewis the iron merchant.

**These have been read off the page and set out on a working sheet, but not yet imported.** They want checking first, and two readings in particular: a servant given as Harriett Leush, another as Clara Softy, and a third whose forename reads Omah Swaine.

**One schedule may not belong here at all.** Schedule 110, Thomas Walker's, heads the street 'Road North' rather than Cavendish Crescent North.

questions.title: John George Woodward in 1881: 33 Cavendish Road East, or Carisbrooke House?
questions.detail:
**The record has him alone at 33 Cavendish Road East for 1881.** The 1881 schedule 106 has him at Carisbrooke House on Cavendish Crescent North with eight others: his wife Caroline, his stepson Lewis H E de Vera, an architect of 28, three grown children, and three servants.

**Both cannot be right.** If the schedule is right, his existing row wants moving rather than duplicating, and the other eight creating alongside it. The stepson is the useful name here, being unusual enough to trace on his own; he is not in the record at all.

questions.title: 13 Park Valley and Sunny Side: two houses the 1891 enumerator walked that the record does not hold
questions.detail:
**There is no 13 Park Valley among the properties**, though the 1891 schedule for it is plain enough and gives Walter Wadsworth and five others. The numbers run 11 and then 15, with nothing between.

**Sunny Side has no property either**, and it held the largest household on the street - fifteen people under John Howard Bradwell.

Both households are now in the record but unfiled, so they can be found and placed once it is known whether these are houses that were later renumbered, renamed, or demolished.

questions.title: 2, 4, 6 and 8 Pelham Crescent are not in the record, but the 1891 enumerator wrote up three of them
questions.detail:
**The record's Pelham Crescent runs 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 10, 11, 12 and upward** - no 2, 4, 6 or 8.

**The 1891 enumerator wrote up schedules for 4, 6 and 8** in a continuous run between houses that do exist, which is hard to explain unless the houses were there. Schedule 9 is Edgar Herbert Hill's at number 4, schedule 7 is Charles Henry Clarke's at 6, and schedule 8 is Alfred Harriman Clarke's at 8. Those seventeen people are in the record but unfiled.

Either the numbering changed, or these are houses that have since gone.

questions.title: 10 Pelham Crescent in 1891: the house number can be read two ways
questions.detail:
**Schedule 6 of the 1891 census carries John Henry Brown's household of eleven**, and the house number on the page supports two different readings, neither decisively. The household has been left unfiled rather than filed on a coin toss.

John Henry Brown is a wine merchant, and appears ten years earlier as head of schedule 88 on the same street, also without a usable house number. Placing either household would place the other.

questions.title: Thorn Lea is 7 Western Terrace, and Lincoln Villa is 11 - both settled from the directory
questions.detail:
**Two 1891 households on Pelham Crescent are given by name rather than number.** Thorn Lea holds eight under George Elinsley Coke; Lincoln Villa holds eleven under Joseph Bright. Neither name is in the record against any property.

Both are the sort of name that ought to resolve to a number from a directory of the 1890s, and Joseph Bright is already in the record, which may make him the quicker way in.

**Thorn Lea stood empty on census night 1901.** The enumerator marked it uninhabited on his round, so the house survived the decade but lost the Cokes. See [[empty-houses-census-night-1901]].

**The 1901 round moves them, and that is the useful part.** Ten years on, the enumerator reaches Lincoln Villa and Thorn Lea **between 10 Western Terrace and the North Road lodge** - schedule 217 is 10 Western Terrace, 218 is Lincoln Villa, Thorn Lea follows, and 220 is the lodge on North Road. In 1891 both were written up as Pelham Crescent.

**It is the same house, not a name reused.** Joseph Bright, solicitor, is at Lincoln Villa in both years - 51 in 1901 with Frances, Horace, Josephine and Frank, and the same family ten years earlier. So the household did not move and the name did not travel; what changed is which street the enumerator wrote at the head of the schedule.

**So both houses sit near where Pelham Crescent, Western Terrace and North Road meet**, and are addressed off whichever the enumerator was working along. That is a much smaller search than "somewhere on Pelham Crescent", and it is the same corner problem as [[kentmere-ccn]], where a house on the join of two crescents is written up under either.

**Thorn Lea stood empty on census night 1901**, so the Cokes had gone by then - see [[empty-houses-census-night-1901]].

**Answered, and from a source already in the record.** Wright's Directory for 1894-95 prints, on **Western Terrace**: *no. 7, Thorn lea, George E. Coke, of Coke, Mills & Coke*. That is the same George Elinsley Coke the 1891 census gives at Thorn Lea, with a house number against his name.

**So Thorn Lea is 7 Western Terrace.** The reasoning above - that it sat somewhere near the junction of Pelham Crescent, Western Terrace and North Road, addressed off whichever street the enumerator was walking - was sound as far as it went, and is now beside the point. The 1891 schedule heading it Pelham Crescent was simply wrong.

**Lincoln Villa is 11 Western Terrace (#350)**, which the record already carried as that property's house name. The directory confirms it independently for 1910-11, 1913-14 and 1915-16, where Sir Joseph Bright J.P. and his sons Arthur Stanley and Horace Dickinson are all printed at Lincoln Villa, Western Terrace - the same family the 1891 and 1901 censuses give.

**What remains.** Western Terrace runs 1 to 11 in the record, and #346 is 7 Western Terrace. The Coke household of 1891 should be filed there once somebody is satisfied the numbering has not shifted since 1894.

questions.title: Pelham Cottage and Pelham Cottages: where on the crescent were they?
questions.detail:
**Three separate 1881 schedules are headed Pelham Cottage** - Fletcher Hind's four, Johnson Marriott's two, and Charles Sidney Hill alone - and two more in 1891 are headed Pelham Cottages, holding Ethel Matilda Pitts's three and Sarah Warriner's five.

The name is in the record nowhere. Small dwellings of this sort often stood behind or beside the larger houses, and the Hinds at least are already in the record, so they may be placeable from another source.

questions.title: The 1881 Lenton Avenue enumerator numbered almost nothing
questions.detail:
**Eleven of his seventeen households carry no house number at all**, only the street - among them Joseph Thornley the lace manufacturer employing over two hundred hands, John Heeley with a household of ten, and Thomas C Moore. Those fifty-four people are in the record but unfiled.

**His walk is the only evidence of order that exists.** He wrote the houses up in sequence, and six of them he did number, so the unnumbered ones sit between fixed points. Working out from those six may place the rest without any further source.

questions.title: Henry Meade Brown, aged 56 in 1891, is entered as the son of a head aged 53
questions.detail:
**The 1891 schedule gives him as Son, aged 56, in a household whose head is 53.** The age has been checked against the page more than once and is what is written there.

It has been recorded unchanged rather than quietly corrected, because the contradiction is the interesting part. Either the enumerator wrote an age into the wrong line, or the relationship column is wrong and he is a brother or a lodger, or the head's own age is understated.

questions.title: Six houses in The Park stood empty on census night 1901
questions.detail:
**The 1901 enumerator marked six houses uninhabited** as he walked: **Blantyre** and **Peveril House** on Cavendish Crescent North, **Ivanhoe** on Peveril Drive, **Thorn Lea** on Pelham Crescent, one house on **Lincoln Circus**, and one on **Park Ravine**.

This is worth having written down because an empty house explains a gap that would otherwise look like a missing page. Thorn Lea in particular is a name the record does not hold against any property, and it held eight people in 1891 under George Elinsley Coke - so it emptied between the two censuses.

questions.title: Frances M. H. Churchill, aged 5, is entered as a daughter of John C. Wright but under another surname
questions.detail:
**At schedule 237 on Peveril Drive in 1901**, John C. Wright, a commercial traveller of 36, is returned with his wife Florence and four children born at Arnold - Dorothy, Rachael and John, all surnamed Wright, and then Frances M. H. **Churchill**, aged 5, also given as Daughter and also born at Arnold.

A stepchild, an adopted child, or a niece written into the wrong column. The birthplace matching the others makes a clerical slip less likely than a real family story.

questions.title: Three birthplaces in the record carry the wrong county
questions.detail:
**Long Eaton is written as Nottinghamshire.** It is in Derbyshire, just over the county line.

**Heckington is given as Leicestershire.** It is in Lincolnshire.

**Stourbridge appears twice, once as Staffordshire and once as Worcestershire.** It was in Worcestershire.

These matter more than they look, because birthplaces are geocoded for the Origins map and a wrong county sends the pin to the wrong place - or, where the name exists in both counties, to a village nobody in the record ever came from.

questions.title: The house names the 1901 census used - seven now placed from the directory, two still missing
questions.detail:
**The 1901 enumerator wrote house names where the record keeps numbers**, and nine of the names he used appear nowhere in the property list, on any street:

**Fairfield**, **Oakleigh**, **Glendale**, **Beechwood** and **Douglas House** on Hamilton Drive; **Lea Hurst** and **Holm Vale** on Fishpond Drive; **Gardenwood** on Clumber Road; and **St John's**, on the stretch between Newcastle Circus and Maxtoke Road.

**These are not small households.** Lea Hurst held ten people under Mary Metcalf, a widow keeping six boarders - a leather merchant, two mechanical engineers, two bank clerks and an architect. Beechwood held nine, among them boarders from Switzerland and Curacao. Oakleigh held nine under Ralph J. Horner, a professor of music, with his son another professor of music.

**Hamilton Drive is the sharpest case.** The record holds sixteen properties there, numbered 1 to 11 with 1a, 1b, 1c, then 24, and Ferndene. The 1901 round gives thirteen households on that street and names five of them, and not one name matches. So either the houses were renamed between 1901 and whenever the record's numbering was set, or the numbered properties and the named ones are different buildings.

**Until a name is tied to a number, every one of these households stays unfiled.** A directory of the 1900s printing a name against a number would place a household of ten at a stroke, and Ralph Horner, professor of music, is the sort of resident a directory prints.

**ANSWERED IN LARGE PART, from Wright's Directory - a source already transcribed in this record.** Reading each house name together with the street it is printed under settles seven of the nine, four of them with a number:

- **Douglas House is 10 Hamilton Drive** - Alfred Clarke, civil engineer, 1894-95 and 1898-99; Benjamin R. Tomlinson, lace manufacturer, by 1910-11.
- **Oakleigh is on Hamilton Drive** - D. M. F. Gaskin, the Corporation water engineer, in 1894-95, and **Ralph Horner, mus. bac.**, in 1898-99. That is the professor of music the 1901 census gives at Oakleigh with his son.
- **Glendale is on Hamilton Drive** - John T. Roseblade, corn merchant's traveller, in both volumes, the same head the 1901 round gives.
- **Lea Hurst is on Fish Pond Drive** - Mrs Mary Metcalf in 1898-99, the widow with six boarders on the 1901 return; Arthur Hutchinson by 1910-11; and by 1913-14 it is Godfrey Walter's **boarding house** outright, which explains the household of ten.
- **Holm Vale is on Fish Pond Drive** - William E. Sisling, insurance manager, with Miss F. Sisling, 1898-99: the same household as 1901.
- **Leslie House is 31 Lenton Road** and **Yeldersley House is 43 Lenton Road** - Henry Clark the lace manufacturer and George Hicking of G. & W. N. H., both the heads the 1901 round gives.
- **Newlands is 33 Lenton Avenue**, which the census sheet already said.

**Two names appear in no volume at all: Fairfield and Beechwood**, both on Hamilton Drive, along with **Gardenwood** on Clumber Road and **St John's**. Beechwood is the lodging house of nine with boarders from Switzerland and Curacao; a house of that kind may have been let rather than owned, which is one reason a directory might pass over it.

**The two "clashes" were not clashes, and I was wrong to call them so.** The directory holds **two Cavendish Houses** - one on Cavendish Road East, Charles Sudbury's and later Mrs Marina Sudbury's, and a separate one on **Fish Pond Drive**, where **Charles O. Terry, insurance broker**, is printed in 1898-99. Terry is the exact head of the 1901 Fish Pond Drive schedule, so that household belongs at a Fish Pond Drive house of that name, not at #56. And **Burton House is on Maxtoke Road**, where Mrs Elizabeth A. Watson is printed in 1894-95 and 1898-99 - the same widow as the 1901 schedule. The record's Burton House on Newcastle Circus (#205) is a different building.

**What is now wanted** is not more sources but the work of matching: several of these names have no property in the record at all - Oakleigh, Glendale, Lea Hurst, Holm Vale, Cavendish House on Fish Pond Drive - and want creating before the households sitting unfiled can be placed against them.

**HAMILTON DRIVE: four numbers now have names against them.** A. Hagues has identified **1c as Ivy Nook** and **3 as Warwick House** from the houses themselves, and photographed the gate piers at **10, which reads WISTERIA HOUSE** today. The record already carried Wisteria House at #123, so the photograph confirms what was held rather than adding to it.

**And that settles Douglas House.** Wright's Directory prints *Douglas house, no. 10* on Hamilton Drive in 1894-95 (Alfred Clarke, civil engineer) and again in 1898-99, and Benjamin R. Tomlinson there by 1910-11. So **10 Hamilton Drive was Douglas House and is now Wisteria House** - one building under two names - and the 1901 household at Douglas House belongs to **#123**: Alice Clarke, a widow of 47 living on private means, with two Naylor visitors and a servant. She is #4257 in the record with an unfiled row, so this is a reassignment rather than an import.

**Alice is very likely Alfred's widow**, the directory having him at that house through the 1890s and the census giving her there alone on private means in 1901. The record holds no Alfred Clarke who fits - the three it has are a lace manufacturer born 1850, a schoolmaster born 1865 and a son born 1882 - so the civil engineer is absent from it, and the relationship is an inference rather than a fact until a marriage or a death notice says so.

**Three named houses on that street still have no number**: Fairfield (John H. Jackson, fruit salesman), Oakleigh (Ralph Horner) and Glendale (John T. Roseblade). The directory gives the street for all three but prints no number against them.

**And Beechwood appears twice on the 1901 round** - once unnumbered under Sarah Wilkinson, and again at schedule 85 as a lodging house of nine with boarders from Switzerland and Curacao. Two houses of one name, or one household my reading of the page split in two. It wants looking at before either is placed.

**The numbers still unaccounted for on Hamilton Drive** are 1, 1a, 1b, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 11, against which the round offers Fairfield, Oakleigh, Glendale, Beechwood and six households the enumerator left unnamed.

**The OS sheet adds two Hamilton Drive names and confirms Ivy Nook.** A. Hagues's 1:1250 extract marks **Ivy Nook** on Hamilton Drive, which he places at 1c, and gives **Clovelly** and **The Limes** on the north side beside Ferndene. None of the three is in the property record. It does not name Fairfield, Oakleigh, Glendale or Beechwood, so those four remain without a number from any source - map, directory or census.

**GLENDALE IS A BUILDING OF SEVERAL DWELLINGS, NOT ONE HOUSE.** A. Hagues has read the 1901 return at source on TheGenealogist, and the House column for Hamilton Drive gives, in order: **Glendale** (Alice M Roseblade), **Glendale** (Frank Hodson), **6 Glendale** (Walter Woodward), **7 Glendale** (Florence Cockburn). All on piece 3165.

So the numbers belong to the building, not to the street. **6 Glendale is not 6 Hamilton Drive**, and the two households cannot be filed at #119 and #120 on the strength of those figures - a mistake this note previously made and which is corrected here.

- **6 Glendale** - Walter Woodward, timber merchant and employer, 44; his housekeeper Mary Scotney; a visiting bank manager, William J. Pearce, with Annie E. Pearce; and a servant. Five people.
- **7 Glendale** - Florence Cockburn, 34, born at Rugby; her aunt Elizabeth Horsley on private means; a nephew, Herbert G. Neil, a lace warehouseman born in Scotland; a boarding chemical student, James J. Wedgwood; and a servant. Five people.

**This is why the earlier conflict would not reconcile.** John J. Roseblade at Glendale and Woodward and Cockburn at 6 and 7 are not competing for one house: they are neighbours in one building. The directory printing *Glendale, John T. Roseblade* on Hamilton Drive in 1894-95 and 1898-99 names the building, as directories generally do, without saying which part of it he held.

**A discrepancy in the head.** TheGenealogist gives **Alice M Roseblade** as head of the unnumbered Glendale household; the enumerator's page as read here gives **John. J. Roseblade**, 51, a corn merchant's agent, with daughters Emily, Alice and May Victoria, two French boarders and two servants. Alice is eighteen on that page and a school teacher's assistant, so she is unlikely to be its head. Either the index names a different person of the household, or there are two Roseblade households at Glendale.

**And the count does not agree.** TheGenealogist shows **nine households on Hamilton Drive** for 1901; my reading of the enumerator's pages gives thirteen. Some of mine are very likely on neighbouring streets, carried onto this tab because the schedules gave a house name and no street.

All ten are already in the record with unfiled rows, so they want reassigning rather than importing.

**A possible duplicate at number 7.** The record holds a 1921 resident of #120 as **Florence Coctbrand** - which reads like a misreading of Cockburn. If it is the same woman twenty years on, she is one person entered twice under a mangled surname. Worth checking before the 1901 row is filed, so the two are joined rather than left as strangers in the same house.

**And an unresolved conflict about Glendale.** A. Hagues reads Glendale as covering 6 and 7 Hamilton Drive. But the 1901 round puts **Glendale at schedule 80 under John J. Roseblade**, corn merchant's agent, with eight people - and Wright's Directory prints *Glendale, John T. Roseblade* on Hamilton Drive in both 1894-95 and 1898-99. Roseblade cannot be at 6 or 7 on census night if Woodward and Cockburn are.

So either **Glendale is a building name covering more houses than the two**, in the way Ferndene shares a structure with 6 and 7 Peveril Drive, or Roseblade's household sits at another number on the street and the name has moved. Nothing is filed at Glendale until that is settled.

**FOUR OF THE THIRTEEN ARE GLENDALE HOUSEHOLDS.** Set against A. Hagues's reading of the source, my transcription of the Hamilton Drive round names Glendale only once. The source gives four:

- **Glendale** - the Roseblade household of eight, schedule 80.
- **Glendale** - **Frank Hodson**, builder and stone merchant, 47, with his wife Mary, five children from nineteen down to a baby, and a servant. Nine people. My reading has them under the street alone, the schedule number never captured because the page headed them only "Next schedule".
- **6 Glendale** - Walter Woodward's five.
- **7 Glendale** - Florence Cockburn's five.

Twenty-seven people in one building, which for a group of late Victorian villas is entirely plausible and explains why the name recurs across the round without contradiction.

**That probably accounts for the count as well.** TheGenealogist shows nine households on Hamilton Drive against my thirteen; if the four Glendale entries are indexed differently, or if some of my thirteen sit on Peveril Drive or Kenilworth Road - the same corner problem that put Thorndale in two streets at once - the difference closes.

**Beechwood is the one that does not resolve.** My reading has it twice, under Sarah Wilkinson with five people and at schedule 85 under Mary Pearson with nine, and it is not among the four houses the source names on this street. Two houses of one name, one household split by my reading of the page, or a house on a neighbouring street: still open.

**BEECHWOOD, IN FULL, FOR WHOEVER GOES BACK TO THE SOURCE.** The two households my reading gives under this name:

**Schedule 85** - nine people, and not a family at all but a lodging house. Mary Pearson, 37, a professional sick nurse on her own account, is the first named and is entered as a **boarder**, so the head is not among them - the page gives no head at all, which is itself a sign the household was split across a page turn. With her: Arthur H. Niblett, 32, civil engineer, from Gloucestershire; George W. Sellars, 33, lace warehouseman, born Switzerland; **Fritz Firmenich, 26, chemical manufacturer, and Hugo Firmenich, 20, lace warehouseman, both Swiss**; Henry Perevia, 27, commercial traveller, born **Curacao**; Maurice Potter, 43, merchant and employer, from Skirbeck in Lincolnshire; and two servants, Elizabeth Burrows and Florence Tett.

**No schedule captured** - five people, and a family: Sarah Wilkinson, 52, born at Burnaston in Derbyshire, with two sons and two daughters, all four born at Newark, the sons a grocer's assistant and a grocer's warehouseman.

**Firmenich is the name to search.** Two Swiss brothers in one Nottingham lodging house is about as distinctive as an index entry gets, and finding them settles which house Beechwood is, whether the two households share it, and whether the nine-person entry is one household or the tail of another. Henry Perevia of Curacao is nearly as good.

**THE WILKINSONS, AND WHY THEY ARE NOT YET PLACED.** A. Hagues finds a **Wilkinson household at Derby House, 1 Derby Terrace** - but in the **1911** return, not 1901. That is worth setting down carefully, because the two do not automatically join up:

- **Derby House is #97 in the record, and holds nobody in any year.** Whatever is at it in 1911 would be new.
- **The record has no 1911 Wilkinson household at all.** Its only two Wilkinsons that year are Sarah Elizabeth, a domestic servant of 28 at #239, and a Daisy at #34. So a family at Derby House in 1911 is genuinely missing, not misfiled.
- **The 1901 household stands apart.** Sarah Wilkinson, born about 1849, a widow of 52 from Burnaston in Derbyshire, with William 22, Florence 26, Maybell 24 and Stuart 17, all four born at Newark. She would be 62 in 1911.

**Nothing is filed on this yet.** A household ten years later at a house the record does not otherwise hold is a good lead and not a placement: the 1901 schedule would need to name Derby House, or the 1911 one to name the same children, before the two are joined. Until then the 1901 rows keep the Beechwood label my reading gave them, which is very likely wrong - the name probably belongs to the household that follows.

**A visitor my reading lost.** The original transcription of that 1901 household ends with **Alissimon Hopewell, visitor, 36**. She is in the record as **#1143, born 1864** - which matches 36 in 1901 exactly - but only from the **1921** return, as wife of Frank Handley Hopewell at #346. So the record holds the woman and lacks her 1901 row, which my parser dropped when it split the household. Six people, not five.

**BEECHWOOD IS ANSWERED, AND IT IS ONE HOUSEHOLD, NOT TWO.** The 1911 return supplied by A. Hagues gives **Sarah Wilkinson, 62, widow, born Burnaston in Derbyshire - a BOARDING HOUSE KEEPER** - at Derby House, 1 Derby Terrace, with thirteen people under her roof: her daughter Florence, a daily governess; eight boarders; and four servants whose occupations are written out as cook, kitchen maid and housemaids **of the boarding house**.

**That settles what the 1901 page was doing.** My reading split Beechwood into two households: Sarah Wilkinson with four children, and a separate group of nine beginning with Mary Pearson. The second had **no head at all** and began with somebody entered as a *boarder*, which I noted at the time as a sign of a page turn. It was. Sarah is the head; the nine are her lodgers; it is a single household of about fifteen, and she was keeping a boarding house at Beechwood in 1901 as she was at Derby House ten years later.

So the lodgers of 1901 - Arthur Niblett the civil engineer, George Sellars, **Fritz and Hugo Firmenich**, Henry Perevia of Curacao, Maurice Potter the merchant, and the servants Elizabeth Burrows and Florence Tett - belong with the Wilkinsons, and the household wants rejoining.

**She moved between the censuses.** Beechwood is on Hamilton Drive and Derby House on Derby Terrace, so these are two houses, not one renamed. A boarding-house keeper moving premises in ten years is unremarkable, and it means Beechwood still needs a number on Hamilton Drive - but it is no longer a mystery about who lived there.

**The 1911 household is new to the record.** Derby House (#97) holds nobody in any year, and the record has no 1911 Wilkinson household, so all thirteen would be created.

**AND A POSSIBLE NAME FOR IT.** A. Hagues recalls a **Beechdale House** on Peveril Drive near the Hamilton Drive corner, and has someone in Nottingham going to look. One syllable from Beechwood, on the corner that has already put Thorndale in two streets at once. See [[beechdale-house-peveril-corner]].

questions.title: The 1901 round is 102 schedules of 243 - what is still to read, and which gap matters most
questions.detail:
**The 1901 enumerator's round runs from schedule 6 to schedule 248, and the record now holds 102 of them.** The rest have not been read. The gaps, as runs:

**8 to 73** - sixty-six households, much the largest hole, and the one that would give Hamilton Drive, Kenilworth Road and Fish Pond Drive their neighbours. Perhaps three hundred people.

**150 to 179** - thirty households, and the run that matters most for a filing already made. A. Hagues reads this stretch as Ernest Jardine, then 6 Clumber Road, then Hesse, then Felixstowe, then the Kippings - which is why the Kipping household is filed at Holly Lodge. Those pages would prove that order or break it. They would also give Clumber Road properly: the record holds two households there for 1901 where the street has eleven properties.

**129 to 134**, **90 to 96**, **212 to 216** - six, seven and five households.

Then single schedules and short runs: 81-84, 98-100, 107, 112-114, 121-123, 141-143, 187, 191, 193, 219, 227, 239, 241-243, 245.

**Why the numbering has holes at all.** Some are houses returned uninhabited, which the enumerator numbered and left empty - six of those are known and recorded in [[empty-houses-census-night-1901]]. The rest are simply pages not yet read.

**The order to take them in**, on present evidence: 150-179 first, because it settles a filing that currently rests on inference rather than on a page; then 8-73, because it is the largest and three streets depend on it.

questions.title: Park Mount is on Park Drive, and was Otto Homberger’s for twenty years
questions.detail:
**Answered from Wright's Directory, which prints it in every volume held.** *Park mount, Otto Homberger, of Homberger & Co.* appears on **Park Drive** in 1894-95 and 1898-99, and *Homberger Otto (Homberger & Co)* at the same house in 1910-11, 1913-14 and 1915-16. Twenty-one years in one house.

**The 1901 census agrees.** Schedule 222 of that round is headed *Park Drive, "Park Mount"* and gives Otto Homberger, a lace merchant of 49, a German subject naturalised British, with his wife Kate and three servants.

**The record holds no property called Park Mount.** Park Drive has nine - numbered 1 to 9 with Ashley House and Clumber House among them - and none carries the name. So either it is one of those under a name the record has not kept, or it is a house the property list does not hold.

**Kate Homberger is the reason this matters beyond the house.** Her marriage bears on the Dowson household at Felixstowe, and Otto is one of the German lace merchants whose naturalisation the record deliberately keeps in the birthplace field. A. Hagues has said the house may be identifiable on foot.

**Until it is placed**, the 1901 household stays unfiled - see [[1901-house-names-not-in-the-record]] for the others in the same position.

questions.title: Derby House: the Wilkinsons found at Newark, and which sister went to Australia?
questions.detail:
**A Lenton memoir describes the house from the outside, and confirms three things the censuses only imply.** A recollection of Hermon Street published at lentontimes.co.uk remembers Derby House, across Derby Road, as an **upper-class boarding house owned by a Miss Wilkinson**, where the writer earned pocket money helping in the kitchen on Sundays. It names the chef as **Mr Bird**; says the property was later taken by **the Lace Marketing Board**; and recalls that during the war the writer's family swapped margarine for **tinned fruit that Miss Wilkinson's sister sent from Australia**.

**Mr Bird is in the record.** **William Alfred Bird**, born 1892 at Carlton in Nottinghamshire, is a servant in the house on the 1921 census at 28 and a manservant on the 1939 register at 47. The memoir gives him the trade the official returns do not: he was the cook. Eighteen years in one house, and now a name with a job attached.

**"A Miss Wilkinson" fits either sister, and the war years point to Maybell.** Sarah, the mother, was keeping the house at 72 in 1921 and is not on the 1939 register, so she had died or given it up by then. On that register **Maybell Martina** is the proprietress and **Florence Allissinon May** is retired, both single - so a wartime recollection of "Miss Wilkinson" is most likely Maybell.

**But then who is the sister in Australia?** The 1901 household holds only two daughters, Florence born 1874 and Maybell born 1876, with sons William born 1879 and Stuart born 1884. Both daughters are in the house in 1939. So either:

- there was a **third daughter**, older or born in the gap between 1879 and 1884, who had left home before the 1901 census and emigrated - the record would have no trace of her at all; or
- **Florence went to Australia after 1939**, which at 65 and retired is possible but unlikely; or
- the memoir means a sister-in-law, or misremembers the relationship, which reminiscence written down decades later often does.

**Nobody in the record connects to Australia** except the Cartwrights of Melbourne and John Kneebone of South Australia, none of them Wilkinsons.

**What would settle it:** the 1881 or 1891 census for the Wilkinson family at Newark, where all four known children were born, which would give the full set of Sarah's daughters before any of them left home. A passenger list or a probate notice naming an Australian sister would do as well.

**And a date for the end of the house:** the Lace Marketing Board's occupation of Derby House would give the year the boarding house closed, which is currently unknown - the record follows the Wilkinsons to 1939 and no further. See [[1901-house-names-not-in-the-record]] for the Beechwood end of the same story.

**THE WILKINSONS CANNOT BE FOUND AT NEWARK IN 1881 OR 1891.** A. Hagues has looked and they are not there under Sarah's name - which is to be expected, because she was not the head of the household in either year. She is a widow by 1901, so in 1881 and 1891 the household stands under her husband's name and she is listed as his wife. **The record holds no Wilkinson man who could be him**, so he died between 1884, when Stuart was born at Newark, and 1901.

**The way in is not Sarah but the unusual names.** *Maybell* for a daughter born 1876, *Stuart* for a son born 1884 at Newark, and above all **Allissinon**, which the 1921 census gives as Florence's middle name.

**And there is an Allissinon already in this record.** **Alissimon Hopewell (#1143) was born at NEWARK in 1864** - the same town as all four Wilkinson children - and is at #346 in 1921 as the wife of Frank Handley Hopewell of Mansfield. She is the visitor aged 36 whom the 1901 reading of the Beechwood household records, and my parser dropped.

**She cannot be Sarah's daughter.** Sarah was born in 1849 and would have been fifteen in 1864. The likelier relation by far is that **Alissimon was born a Wilkinson** - her husband's sister, Florence's aunt, and the woman Florence was named after. That reading fits the 1901 visit exactly: an aunt calling on her sister-in-law and her nieces, in the boarding house her brother's widow was keeping.

**If that is right, it opens the 1881 census.** Alissimon Wilkinson would be seventeen at Newark in 1881, living with her parents - and her father is Sarah's father-in-law, which finds the family without needing Sarah's married surname to be searchable at all. A marriage registration for Hopewell and Wilkinson would confirm the maiden name outright.

**None of this makes her the Australian sister.** Alissimon is in Nottingham in 1921 as Mrs Hopewell, so the sister who sent tinned fruit through the war is somebody else, and remains unaccounted for.

**FOUND: 3 CHURCH STREET, NEWARK UPON TRENT, 1891.** A. Hagues has the family's Newark address at last, through the youngest child: **Stuart Murray Wilkinson**, 7, born Newark 1884, a scholar. His full name is new - the record holds him only as Stuart - and *Murray* is one more distinctive name to search on.

**But the household as indexed is five people and contains no parent.** Stuart is entered as **Son** with nobody for him to be the son of: a visitor, Mary Wilson of Lincoln, 22, living on her own means; and three servants - Sarah Taylor a nursemaid, Mary Ann Baker a housemaid, and Annie Rastall a cook, all from Lincolnshire. **Florence, Maybell and William are absent too**, though they would be 17, 15 and 12.

**So on census night 1891 the parents were away and the youngest boy was left at home with the staff.** A nursemaid and a cook for one seven-year-old says a household of some means, which fits a family that could later keep an upper-class boarding house.

**That is also why no search for Sarah finds them.** She is not in her own house that night. The next place to look is wherever she and her husband were - and if the husband can be named from the 1891 return for 3 Church Street in an earlier year, or from a directory for Newark, the whole family follows.

**This household is not created in the record.** Newark is not The Park, and the estate's census rows are for houses on it; what belongs here is the fact of the address and the names, not a household at a property the record does not hold.

**Still unaccounted for:** the sister in Australia, and whether Alissimon Hopewell - born Newark 1864, and very likely a Wilkinson by birth - is the aunt Florence was named after.

**THE HUSBAND IS NAMED. 2 & 3 CHURCH STREET, NEWARK UPON TRENT, 1881.** A. Hagues has the household ten years earlier, and at its head is **WILLIAM M WILKINSON, 34, born about 1847, a GROCER EMPLOYING 13 MEN AND 5 BOYS**. Sarah is his wife, 32, born in Derbyshire, which agrees with the Burnaston of every later return.

**A grocer of that size explains a good deal.** Eighteen employees is a substantial business, and it accounts for the household of 1891 - a nursemaid and a cook kept for one seven-year-old boy while his parents were away. It also explains what became of the sons: on the 1901 return **William is a grocer's assistant and Stuart a grocer's warehouseman**, both in their father's trade.

**And it confirms the daughters' names.** They are entered by initials: **F A M**, 6, and **M M**, 4 - Florence Allissinon May and Maybell Martina, exactly as the 1921 census spells them out. Their birth years here are 1875 and 1877, a year later than the 1921 and 1939 figures, which is the ordinary drift of census ages.

**There are only two daughters in 1881.** So a third - the sister who sent tinned fruit from Australia - would have to have been born **after 1881**, in the gap between the son of 1879 and Stuart of 1884, or after Stuart. That is a much smaller search than before.

**One oddity in the household.** The son born 1879 is indexed as **N J S Wilkinson**, aged 2, where the 1901 return gives a son **William**, 22, born the same year. Either the initials are misread, or the boy of 1879 died and another son of the same birth year cannot be the same child. Worth a look, since a son who died young would be one more child to account for.

**William M Wilkinson is not in this record.** He died between 1884, when Stuart was born, and 1901, when Sarah is a widow keeping a boarding house at Beechwood - a fall from grocer of eighteen hands to lodging-house keeper that a death and a failed business would both explain. His death registration would date it, and Newark directories of the 1880s would show how long the firm lasted.

**What is still wanted:** a daughter born after 1881, a death for William M Wilkinson, and confirmation that Alissimon Hopewell - born Newark 1864, and very probably his sister - is the aunt Florence was named after.

**WAS SHE EVER AT BEECHWOOD? A. HAGUES DOUBTS IT, AND THE DOUBT IS WELL FOUNDED.** William M Wilkinson died in **1892**. A widow setting up a boarding house at one address and moving to another within twenty years is possible but wasteful, and the simpler reading is that she went to Derby House and stayed - which is where the record finds her in 1911, 1921 and 1939.

**My own transcription is weaker evidence than I have been treating it as.** The 1901 Wilkinson household carries **no schedule number**; it sits in the gap where schedules 81 to 84 are missing from the pages read; and the house name I gave it is written as a bare label in quotation marks, separate from the entry that follows it - *Sch 85, Beechwood, Hamilton Drive*. So the name may have been taken from the household after theirs rather than from their own line. That is exactly the mistake that put Henry Towle's household on Peveril Drive.

**Three other things already told against Beechwood.** The source A. Hagues consulted counts **nine** households on Hamilton Drive in 1901 where my reading gives thirteen; Beechwood is not among the four houses he found named there; and it appears in **no volume** of Wright's Directory, on that street or any other.

**But one thing tells for it.** **Derby House is 880 metres from Hamilton Drive** - most of the width of the estate, and almost certainly a different enumerator's round. If Sarah were at Derby House in 1901 she should not appear in that sequence at all, and the household was transcribed from a page within it.

**The test is simple and is not mine to make.** The 1901 return for **1 Derby Terrace**: if Sarah Wilkinson is there, the Beechwood label is my error and the family has one boarding house, not two. If somebody else is there, she was elsewhere in 1901 and Beechwood - or whatever that page actually calls the house - stands.

**Until that is known, nothing moves.** The 1901 rows keep the label they have, marked as uncertain, and the three Derby House households stand on their own evidence.

**TESTED, AND BEECHWOOD STANDS.** A. Hagues has looked at the 1901 return and confirms it is the Beechwood household. So the label my transcription gave it was right, the doubt above is closed, and **Sarah Wilkinson did keep two boarding houses in succession**:

- **1892** - William M Wilkinson dies, leaving her a widow with four children between eight and eighteen.
- **1901** - Beechwood, on the Hamilton Drive round, with her four grown children at home and nine lodgers: a civil engineer, two Swiss brothers, a commercial traveller from Curacao, a merchant, a sick nurse and two servants. Fifteen people.
- **1911** - Derby House, 1 Derby Terrace, thirteen people, and her trade written out at last as boarding house keeper.
- **1921** - Derby House still, at seventy-two.
- **1939** - Derby House, her daughter Maybell now proprietress, Florence retired.

**Nine years from widowhood to Beechwood, ten more to Derby House** - which on reflection is not a hurried pair of ventures but a trade she moved premises in once, as any lodging-house keeper might, from a house on the estate to a larger one at its edge.

**So Beechwood is a real house and still wants a number.** It is the last name on the Hamilton Drive round with nothing against it, absent from every volume of Wright's Directory and from the nine households the source counts on that street. The Firmenich brothers remain the most distinctive thing in it to search on.

questions.title: Is there a Beechdale House on Peveril Drive - and is it Beechwood?
questions.detail:
**A. Hagues has a recollection of a house called BEECHDALE HOUSE, and places it on Peveril Drive near the Hamilton Drive corner.** Nothing of that name is in the record - not in the property list, not in any census transcription, not in Wright's Directory, and not on the OS sheet. He has asked someone in Nottingham to walk the corner and look for the name on the house itself. This note is here so that whatever they come back with lands somewhere.

**Why it matters more than a stray name usually would.** Beechwood is the one house name from the 1901 Hamilton Drive round still without a number. It held Sarah Wilkinson's boarding house of about fifteen - her four grown children and nine lodgers, among them the Swiss brothers Fritz and Hugo Firmenich and Henry Perevia of Curacao - before she moved the trade to Derby House by 1911. It appears in no volume of the directory and is not among the nine households the source counts on Hamilton Drive. **Beechdale and Beechwood are one syllable apart**, and a name seen on a gate is exactly the kind of evidence that would settle it.

**And that corner is already known to confuse the two streets.** Thorndale is a corner house numbered on Hamilton Drive and built into the Peveril Drive terrace; the 1901 enumerator wrote it under Peveril Drive. A house standing on Peveril Drive at the Hamilton end could reasonably be written under either street, which would explain why Beechwood cannot be fitted to a Hamilton Drive number and does not appear in the street's directory entries.

**Three things the name could turn out to be.**

- **The same house as Beechwood**, either misread by me on the enumerator's page or renamed since. That places Beechwood on the Peveril Drive side of the corner and closes the oldest open question on that round.
- **A different house altogether**, not in the property record. Peveril Drive already holds two named properties with no number - **Parkdale (#299)** and **Peveril House (#300)** - so an unnumbered named house there is the pattern, not the exception. A third would want creating, and the unnamed Peveril Drive households of 1901 (schedules 236, 237, 238, 240, and the one written under Park Dale at 228) are the candidates for who was in it.
- **Parkdale itself, misremembered.** This is the first thing to rule out. **Parkdale is already in the record on Peveril Drive** with no number against it, and it is a -dale name on the same short stretch. Seeing a plate and recalling it a month later as Beechdale is an easy slip and costs nothing to check.

**WHAT WOULD BE MOST USEFUL FROM NOTTINGHAM.** Not just whether the name is there, but:

1. **Which street the house fronts** - the door and the gate, not the side wall. That is the whole Thorndale problem in one observation.
2. **Whether a number is on the house as well as a name**, and what it is.
3. **Which houses stand either side of it**, named or numbered. Two neighbours fix a house in a row even when its own plate says nothing useful.
4. **A photograph of the plate**, which settles the spelling past any argument - dale or wood.

**In the meantime the record claims nothing.** No property is created, no household moved, and Beechwood stays where the 1901 page put it, on Hamilton Drive without a number.

questions.title: Frank Beckitt Lewis, City Architect of Nottingham, at 6 Lenton Road
questions.detail:
**The record has held him since the 1911 return and nobody has looked at him.** **Frank Beckitt Lewis (#815), born Nottingham 1862**, is entered on the 1911 census at **6 Lenton Road** as *city architect*, living at forty-nine in his father's house. The 1901 return gives the same man at the same house, aged thirty-nine, as **"City Architect (Nottm) (own a/c)"** - so he held the office across at least that decade.

**He is the son of a cork cutter.** **William W Lewis (#3794)** is at 6 Lenton Road in 1891 as a cork cutter and in 1911, at seventy-nine, as a retired lace merchant; Wright's Directory prints him there in 1894-95, 1898-99 and 1910-11. Frank is one of seven children, and the only one who left the family trades - his brothers were a cork cutter's assistant and a yarn agent's assistant.

**He is absent from the house in 1891**, aged twenty-nine, which is where a young architect would be: articled, working, or qualifying somewhere else. The 1891 return for wherever he was would give the practice he trained in.

**What is wanted.** The years he held the office, and what he was responsible for. A City Architect of Nottingham in the 1900s is a public appointment with a paper trail - council minutes, the local press, the building control records - and the buildings are likely still standing. Whether any of them are on this estate is the question that matters here.

**And how he was nearly lost.** My transcription of the 1901 page read the enumerator's ditto mark under the surname column as a surname, so he went into the record as **"Frank B."** - a man with no family name, sitting unfiled on Lenton Road. See [[1901-ditto-surnames]]. Four of his household went in the same way, and the house they were in could not be recognised until the surname came back.

questions.title: Nineteen people from the 1901 round entered without a surname - all now resolved
questions.detail:
**An enumerator writing a household does not repeat the surname.** He writes it against the head and rules a ditto mark down the column for everybody under him. My transcription of the 1901 pages read that mark as what stood in the column, so nineteen people went into the record with a **middle initial in place of a family name** - *Frank B.*, *Ellen T.*, *Annie E.*, *Marjorie P.* - each one a person with no surname, sitting unfiled, and unrecognisable as a member of the household they were returned in.

**They are resolved.** Every one has been traced back to the head of the house they were returned under - by schedule number where the page gives one, and where it does not, by the house number written into the address and the head the record already holds filed there.

| entered as | belongs to | already in the record |
|---|---|---|
| Annie E., Arthur E., Marjorie P., Kathleen W. | Joseph Blythe, coachman, **6 Lenton Avenue** | yes - all four |
| Henry C., Arthur J. | Henry Thompson, gardener, **8 Lenton Avenue** | yes - both |
| Margaret A., Katharine J. | Helen M. Parkin, **14 Lenton Avenue** | yes - both |
| Alice M. | Henry Rawson, **12 Lenton Avenue** | yes |
| Lisle N. | William Robinson, **21 Lenton Avenue** | yes |
| Margaret E. | William Bowers, **Lenton Avenue** | no - wants renaming |
| Amy M. | Arthur Forman, newspaper proprietor, **13 Lenton Road** | yes |
| Ellen T., Frank B., Elizth B., Edith C. | William W Lewis, **6 Lenton Road** | yes - all four |
| Mary D., Geoffrey C. | Louisa Heather Williams, **Lenton Road** | no - want renaming |
| Jane A. B. | William Martin, **Hamilton Drive** | no - wants renaming |

**Sixteen of the nineteen are duplicates**, not new people: the record already held them, under their proper names, from a neighbouring census. Only three want a rename - Jane A. Martin, Margaret Bowers, and Mary and Geoffrey Williams.

**One of them matters more than the rest.** *Frank B.* is **Frank Beckitt Lewis**, City Architect of Nottingham. See [[frank-beckitt-lewis-city-architect]].

**And the error was worth having**, because undoing it named three whole households and the houses they were in - Lewis at 6 Lenton Road, Williams on Lenton Road, Bowers on Lenton Avenue - each of which the record already carried in the censuses either side of 1901, and none of which could be matched while the family name was missing.

**The transcription rule this sets.** A ditto mark is not a value. Where a page repeats the surname by ruling it down, the surname carried down from the head is what belongs in the column - which is how this record already handles the 1891 and 1911 rounds.

questions.title: 7 Park Valley is Melbrook House - and Park Valley has no house names at all
questions.detail:
**SETTLED. 7 Park Valley is Melbrook House.** The 1911 householder wrote *Melbrook House, Park* on the cover of his schedule and no number at all; A. Hagues checked the enumerator's address section, which gives **7 Park Valley**. The number is the official address and the name is what the family called it, and they are the same house.

**The action is to add the name to #263** - Map, click the house, House Names, Edit. The year is 1911 from this return; whether it was called that earlier or later is not yet known, so the years are best left open.

**WHAT IS NOT SETTLED IS THE REST OF THE STREET.** Not one of Park Valley's eighteen properties has a house name in the record - where Peveril Drive has Parkdale and Peveril House, and Hamilton Drive has Ferndene. A street of named Victorian villas carrying nothing but numbers is far likelier a gap in the record than a fact about the street, and Melbrook House turning up on the first cover anybody read is the evidence for that.

**Wright's Directory is the place to look**, and it is already transcribed into this record. It prints house names against householders where it has them. One pass down its Park Valley entries would probably name several houses at once.

**And a family question beside it.** The 1901 head of number 7 is **Alfred Wilson, 81**, living on means with his widowed daughter Alice Lynam. The 1911 head is **John Croshaw Wilson, 35**, a hosiery manufacturer. Forty-six years and the same surname in the same house: grandfather and grandson would fit, and nothing in the record says so. *Croshaw* is carried as a middle name by both daughters, which makes the family easy to follow.

See [[1901-house-names-not-in-the-record]] for the same problem on Hamilton Drive.

questions.title: Park Valley jumps from 11 to 15 - and a 1911 household lives in the gap
questions.detail:
**The record's Park Valley runs 1 to 11 and then 15, 17, 19, 21, 23, 25 and Valley House. There is no 12, 13 or 14.** Nothing in the property list has ever occupied those numbers.

**But a 1911 household does.** The schedule of **George Benedict Kohn** - 53, single, lace merchant, export merchant and managing director, born at Beeston - gives a Park Valley number falling in that gap. A. Hagues reads it as 12; the postal address line reads as 12 or 13 and I cannot separate them. He keeps two servants in twelve rooms.

**So the household cannot be filed**, and it is parked in the 1911 transcription rather than put in an import file. Filing it would mean creating a property on the strength of one address line.

**Three things it could be.** The houses existed and were later demolished or absorbed. Or the numbering was revised and what was 12 is now something else. Or the number is a misreading - though 1 to 11 are all accounted for in 1911 by other schedules, which argues against it.

**What would settle it.** Wright's Directory prints Park Valley householders by number and is already in this record: a 12 or a 13 there and the houses existed. The OS 1:1250 sheet would show how many buildings stand between 11 and 15.

**And the head is already half in the record.** George Benedict Kohn is very probably **#3017 Benedict Kohn, born 1858**, a son of the Kohn household at 11 Pelham Crescent on the 1901 round. See [[melbrook-house-park-valley]] for the other Park Valley address question.

questions.title: Arundel Preston of 1 Park Valley: one man, or a man and his widow of the same name?
questions.detail:
**The 1911 schedule and the record disagree about whether Arundel Preston is a man.**

The record holds **#4027 Arundel Preston, born 1838** - head of 1 Park Valley on the 1901 round at 63, a **widower**, occupation *Gentleman*, born in Wiltshire.

The 1911 schedule for the same house gives **Arundel Preston, head, aged 73, widow**, with the age in the **females** column, born at Tisbury in Wiltshire. It is signed *Arundel Preston*.

**Sixty-three to seventy-three is exactly ten years** and Tisbury is in Wiltshire, so on age and birthplace the two are one person.

**Two readings.** Either the age went into the wrong column and *widow* is loose for widower - both common on a householder's own schedule - or Arundel Preston died in the decade and his widow, also called Arundel, took the house. The second is less strange than it sounds, because **his daughter is Arundel Aplin**: the family uses the name for women. But he was already a widower in 1901, so it would need a second marriage after 63.

**The first reading is much the simpler**, and nothing has been changed on the strength of either. The 1911 row is bound to #4027 by number, which is right either way, and no sex is sent.

**What would settle it:** a death registration for Arundel Preston between 1901 and 1911, or its absence. And the return brings a generation the record has never held - **Arundel Aplin**, a widowed daughter of 42, with granddaughters **Alys Arundel** and **Alfreda Althea Aplin**, 11 and 9. No Aplin is in the record at all.

questions.title: Three Bradleys on one short street - brothers?
questions.detail:
**Park Terrace holds three Bradley households across four censuses and the record connects none of them.**

- **Charles Bradley**, born 1842, retired surgeon, head of **3 Park Terrace** in 1891.
- **Herbert Bradley**, born 1848, a **boarder at 10 Park Terrace** in 1891, then head of **3 Park Terrace** in 1901, 1911 and 1921 - unmarried, on private means, with a housekeeper and a housemaid.
- **Alfred Bradley**, born 1846, cotton yarn manufacturer, head of **Broxtowe House** on the same street in 1891, 1901 and 1911, unmarried, keeping house with his niece.

**Born 1842, 1846 and 1848, all in Nottingham, all on one short street**, two of them unmarried, and Herbert takes over the house Charles had. Brothers is the obvious reading and nothing in the record says so.

**Alice Margaret Gill is the way in.** She is Alfred's niece, so one of her parents was a Bradley, and a marriage of a Bradley daughter to a Gill would name the generation above all three men. She is in the record across 1901, 1911 and 1921 with her birth year consistent at 1873.

**A fourth Bradley sits apart:** Frederick James, born 1846, at 15 Pelham Crescent in 1901 and 8 Western Terrace after, with a wife and children.

**There is a duplicate to clear first** - the record holds Herbert Bradley twice, #1796 born 1848 and #4923 born 1849, a year apart and so invisible to the duplicates page.

questions.title: The Ashworths had four children and lost one - was it Leslie?
questions.detail:
**The 1911 return states it and no other source would.** Blanche Isabel Ashworth of 9 Park Valley answers the marriage questions: married thirteen years, **four children born alive, three still living, one died**.

Three are in the house - Edna Blanche Wilson (10), Harold John Vincent (8) and Elaine Isabel (5).

**The record holds a fourth.** **Leslie F. H. Ashworth, born 1900** (#4548), from the 1901 round at Park Ravine, where his parents were before they moved. He appears nowhere in the record after that and is not in this house at eleven years old.

**He is very probably the child who died**, and a death registration would date it. A child who lives and dies between two censuses leaves almost no other trace, and without the 1911 marriage questions nobody would have known to look.

**A correction comes with it.** The record has the eldest daughter as **Edith B. W. Ashworth**, born 1901; the schedule writes her **Edna Blanche Wilson Ashworth** - same initials, same year. Edna read as Edith.

**And the father is in the record under a short form**: **#4546 Fredk J. Ashworth**, born 1873, at Park Ravine in 1901. He is Frederick John Ashworth, timber importer, born at Beeston.

questions.title: Tinsley Lindley of 14 Park Terrace - barrister, and something else
questions.detail:
**The record holds him at one house across three censuses and says only that he was a barrister.** #1819 Tinsley Lindley, born 1866 at Nottingham, head of **14 Park Terrace** in 1901, 1911 and 1921. He signs the 1911 schedule himself in a clear hand - *Tinsley Lindley* - which is worth saying, because the 1921 transcription made him **Tinster Lindey**.

**The name is very unusual and he was a public figure.** A Tinsley Lindley of Nottingham, born in the 1860s, played football for England in the 1880s while qualifying for the bar. Whether that is this man is not something this record can settle on its own, but the name, the town and the dates all point one way, and the record should either establish it or rule it out - because the coincidence will be noticed again by somebody else.

**What would settle it:** an obituary, a bar admission record, or the Nottingham press, which would have noticed either a famous footballer or a well-known barrister living on The Park.

**Twelve people in this record carry the notable mark.** If this is the same man he is an obvious thirteenth.

**His family is small and settled.** Married about 1896, and the 1911 return gives **one child born alive, one still living** - Victoria, four on the 1901 round and the only child they had. **His wife is in the record twice and neither entry is right**: #1820 *Constance Agnes Lindey* has the forename and not the surname, #4785 *Constance Lindley* the surname and not the forename.

questions.title: John Holland Walker of 15 Park Valley - the Nottingham antiquarian?
questions.detail:
**The 1911 schedule for 15 Park Valley is signed John Holland Walker.** He is 37, born at Leeds, and gives his occupation as **department manager in a wholesale clothing factory** - a worker, not an employer. His wife Lucy Mabel is 36, born at Nottingham; married eleven years with no children born. They keep a cook and a house parlourmaid in eleven rooms.

**A J. Holland Walker of Nottingham wrote a great deal on the town's history** in the early twentieth century, including an itinerary of its streets published through the Thoroton Society. The name is uncommon, the town is right, and a man of 37 in 1911 would be of an age to be writing by the 1920s.

**But the trade does not obviously fit**, and that is the whole of the question: the record should not turn a clothing factory manager into an antiquarian because the names agree. Local historians of that generation frequently had day jobs, so it is not evidence against him either.

**What would settle it:** the Thoroton Society's own membership lists or obituaries, which would give an address; or the Nottingham press. An address at 15 Park Valley against the author's name would close it in one line.

**Nobody of this name is in the record**, so whichever way it goes this household is new.

questions.title: James Calvert Wilson, land surveyor to the Newcastle Estate
questions.detail:
**The man who surveyed The Park lived on it.** The 1911 schedule for **Springdale, Clare Valley** gives **James Calvert Wilson**, 49, *land surveyor*, and in the industry column beside it: **Newcastle Estate**.

The record already holds him and his household from the 1911 spreadsheet, but with the trade alone. The employer is the whole of the interest. The Park is the Duke of Newcastle's estate; its layout, its plot boundaries and its numbering were the estate surveyor's work, and this record spends a great deal of effort on exactly those things - which house is which number, where one plot ends and the next begins, why a corner house answers to two streets.

**What is worth finding.** How long he held the post, and what survives of his work. Estate plans, plot books, sale particulars and feu or lease papers are the surveyor's output, and any of them would answer questions this record has open - [[park-valley-12-13-14]] asks whether Park Valley ever had a 12, 13 or 14, and an estate plan would simply show.

**Where such papers would be.** Nottinghamshire Archives holds Newcastle estate material; the Manuscripts and Special Collections at the University of Nottingham hold a great deal more of the Newcastle family's papers.

**He is not a Nottingham man.** Born at Huddersfield, his wife too, and both daughters at Burnley - so he came to the post from Lancashire some time between 1895 and 1911. When he was appointed may itself be findable.

**One correction comes with the schedule:** the record has his servant as *Florence Gertrude Wathing*. The schedule reads **Watkins**.

questions.title: Named houses on the 1911 covers, and which ones the record can already place
questions.detail:
**Six 1911 schedules give a house NAME where the property record works in numbers.** A. Hagues placed four of them from his own knowledge of the estate; two are still open.

| named on the cover | street | where it belongs |
|---|---|---|
| **Melbrook House** | Park Valley | **7 Park Valley**, #263 - from the enumerator's address column |
| **Lynwood** | Tattershall Drive | **2 Tattershall Drive**, #307 |
| **St Ives** | Tattershall Drive | **4 Tattershall Drive**, #309 |
| **Clare Valley Lodge** | Clare Valley | **open** |
| **Elmsdale** | Clare Valley | **5 Clare Valley**, #63 - placed by A. Hagues from the ground |
| **Goddards Lodge** | Tattershall Drive | **open** - and it may settle Elmsdale |
| **Ivy Dene** | Clare Valley | **open** - from the 1901 round, not 1911 |

**Two of the open ones explain households the record has never been able to file.**

- **Clare Valley Lodge.** The 1901 round holds George Hill, a Baptist minister of 53, with his wife and six children, parked unfiled under *Lodge, Clare Valley (no house of that name in the record)*. The 1911 cover names the house outright in the householder's own hand, so the Lodge is real.
- **Elmsdale. SETTLED.** It is **5 Clare Valley**, #63 - the corner house, semi-detached with number 4, which is how the record describes that pair. Arthur Lewis the iron merchant and his family had been unfiled since the 1891 round because Wright's Directory gave two streets and nobody could tell which was meant. **Placing it filed seventeen rows** - eight for 1891, seven for 1901 and two for 1911 - and 5 Clare Valley now holds a continuous line through four censuses where it held only 1921. Emma Elizabeth Goddard heads it in **both 1911 and 1921**, which confirms the placing from inside the record.

**Goddards Lodge may answer that.** The 1911 schedule for Goddards Lodge, Tattershall Drive holds a coachman, and Elmsdale on Clare Valley holds **Emma Elizabeth Goddard**. If the house stands on Clare Valley and its lodge on Tattershall Drive, **the directory was right twice** and the contradiction was never one. The grounds would run between the two roads - which is exactly what 2 and 4 Tattershall Drive do, their gardens reaching Huntingdon Drive. **Not proved. It fits the ground.**

**So several properties want creating**, and four households that have never had a house go to them.

**It is not only these streets.** Park Valley has no house names in the record at all and its numbers jump from 11 to 15 - [[park-valley-12-13-14]], [[melbrook-house-park-valley]]. Hamilton Drive has the same trouble in [[1901-house-names-not-in-the-record]].

**The 1911 covers are the cheapest source of house names there is**, because every household has one and A. Hagues is reading them anyway. On why the ones the record *does* know were hard to find, see [[house-names-live-in-prose]].

**A seventh, from the 1901 round.** *Ivy Dene [?], Clare Valley* holds **George Ranson**, 39, a grocer employing others, his wife Emily, their son of 12 and a servant - four people with no house, under a name the property list does not have. The reading of the name is uncertain, which is why it carries a query, but a household of four is worth placing and the 1911 covers may well name it outright.

questions.title: Are there two Wilkins daughters at 4 Clare Valley, or four?
questions.detail:
**The record holds four Wilkins girls where the house had two.**

The 1901 round gives Lawrence Wilkins, clergyman, at 4 Clare Valley with **Eleanor, born 1896** and **Jessie, born 1897**.

The 1911 schedule for the same house, in their widowed mother's own hand, gives **Joyce, born 1896** and **Mary, born 1897**.

**Same house, same mother, same birth years, different forenames** - and the record holds all four as separate people: #3339 Eleanor, #3340 Jessie, #3344 Joyce, #3345 Mary.

**Two readings.** Either the girls had several forenames and each source picked a different one - entirely ordinary, and *Jessie* is their mother's name, so a daughter called Mary Jessie or Jessie Mary is likely. Or one of the two transcriptions is simply wrong.

**The 1911 names are the better authority**, being the householder's own writing rather than an enumerator's copy. But the 1901 round is A. Hagues's own reading of the page, so this is not a case of trusting a stranger's index over his work.

**What would settle it:** baptisms at St Mary's or wherever Lawrence Wilkins served, which would give each girl's full name at birth. A birth registration would do as well.

**Whichever way it falls, two merges follow**, and the duplicates page cannot see them: the forenames are entirely different, so nothing buckets them together.

**Two other things from that schedule.** Lawrence Wilkins **died between 1901 and 1911** - his widow heads the house. And the fourth child, **L. A. Wilkins**, a son of 6 in 1901, is absent at 16; the marriage answers say four born and four living, so he was alive and elsewhere.

questions.title: The house names the record knows are buried in prose, where nothing can search them
questions.detail:
**There is a `property_names` table and it holds fifteen rows.** For 361 properties.

This came to light the hard way. Two 1911 covers named **Lynwood** and **St Ives**, neither appeared in the property list, and both were written up as houses the record had never held. **A. Hagues placed both immediately** - 2 and 4 Tattershall Drive. The record knew them all along.

**It knew them in the history paragraph**, in sentences like *One of a pair of semi-detached houses c1890. Also known as 'Lynwood'.* That is prose. Nothing on the site can search it, no house page shows the name as a name, and a cover reading *Lynwood* matches nothing.

**St Ives is worse, because the record had already used the name to make a decision.** Dougal de Havilland's Park Map was read at this property and the label sampled was **4StIves** - which is how **T C Hine** came to be accepted as its architect. The name was good enough to attribute a building and still not good enough to find the house by.

**A sweep of the history text turns up 54 properties carrying a quoted house name** - Charnwood, Gleadthorpe, Hazlewood, Brightlands, Cuylerholme, Selsoe, Ferndene, Parkdale, Iveston, Avoca, Fairholme, Oakhurst, Greylands, Newlands, Fern Lodge, Ivanhoe Lodge, Claremont, Napier House, Barton House, Kenilworth House, Redcliffe House, Elmhurst, Overdale and more. **Fifteen are in the table. Roughly forty are not.**

**The fix is mechanical and worth doing before the next round of covers.** Lift the quoted names out of the history text, check each one by eye - the sweep also catches *Bowl*, *Plan for Nottingham Park* and other things that are not house names - and write them into `property_names`, which already has the year_from / year_to columns for a house that changed its name.

**Then every cover name is a lookup instead of a puzzle**, and the open ones in [[clare-valley-missing-houses]] are genuinely open rather than merely unsearchable.

questions.title: Roy Henderson the baritone, aged 11, at 5 Tattershall Drive
questions.detail:
**The record already claimed him. It now has the evidence.**

The description of 5 Tattershall Drive has long said the house *was once occupied by Roy Henderson (1899-2000), popular English baritone in the 1920s, 30s and 40s* - with nothing behind it, and not one member of the family in the record.

**The 1911 schedule is in his father's hand and puts the whole household in the house:**

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| **Alexander Roy Henderson** | 48 | Congregational church minister, born King Edward, Aberdeenshire |
| **Jean Boyd Henderson** | 43 | born Campbeltown, Argyll; married 19 years |
| **Muriel Henderson** | 17 | student, born Montrose |
| **Dorothy Henderson** | 15 | at school, born Edinburgh |
| **Roy Galbraith Henderson** | 11 | at school, born Edinburgh |
| **Kenneth Harvey Henderson** | 4 | born Nottingham |

**Age 11 in April 1911 and born in Edinburgh agrees with a birth in 1899**, and the middle name Galbraith is on the schedule, not supplied from anywhere else.

**What the household adds that a reference book would not.** His father's calling is why the family is in Nottingham at all, and the children's birthplaces date the move - Montrose, then Edinburgh twice, then Nottingham by 1906 or 1907, so Roy came south as a boy of six or seven. **Four children born, four still living.**

**Worth chasing:** which Nottingham congregation Alexander Roy Henderson served - Castle Gate is the obvious candidate and should be checkable in a directory - and whether the family is in the 1921 return at the same address. A minister is also the sort of man the local press reported, so there may be an obituary.

**And the property description should cite this schedule** rather than standing on assertion.

questions.title: Two small Tattershall Drive households whose covers give no number
questions.detail:
**Two 1911 covers read simply *Tattershall Drive* with no number at all**, and both are households quite unlike the rest of the street.

| head | rooms | trade |
|---|---|---|
| **William Henry Holmes**, 41 | 6 | representative to maltsters and yeast merchants; his retired licensed-victualler father and mother living with him |
| **Walter William Jackson**, 33 | 4 | barman at a public house, with a wife, a daughter of 5 and **a boarder** - George William Knott, 57, a widowed piano maker from London |

**Everything else on the street has nine, ten or eleven rooms and servants living in.** These have six and four, no servants, and one of them takes in a lodger. **The Park held both kinds of household at once**, and the record is thinner on the second kind because the big houses are easier to trace.

**Neither can be filed from the schedule**, because the 1911 schedule carries no address - only the cover does, and these two covers were not completed properly. **The enumerator's address column will settle both**, by reading the running order either side of them.

**The likely candidates are the small houses**, not the numbered ones: Carnoustie Lodge, #311, is described in the record as *one of the smallest pre-1918 houses in The Park*, built about 1878-80 **probably as a coachman's house**; Gartree Lodge and Ellington House are the others on the street. **Do not guess between them.** A third small Tattershall Drive household, at Goddards Lodge, names its house and still cannot be placed - [[clare-valley-missing-houses]].

**Do not file any of the three until the address column is read.**

questions.title: Frances May Pearson and Frances Mays Parson - one woman or two?
questions.detail:
**Two women, born the same year, in adjacent houses, in the same census.**

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| **#416 Frances May Pearson** | born 1887 | 1911, property 190 |
| **#858 Frances Mays Parson** | born 1887 | 1911, property 192 |

**Pearson and Parson are one letter apart. May and Mays are one letter apart.** The birth year is identical and the houses are next door but one.
