**Either reading is possible.** Two young women of nearly the same name working in neighbouring houses is perfectly ordinary - service was a local trade and sisters often went into houses on the same street. But so is one woman entered twice from two readings of the same hand.

**The birthplaces would settle it**, and so would the relationship column: two servants are two women, a servant and a daughter are two women, and the same relationship in two houses on one night is impossible.

**The duplicates page cannot decide this** and neither can the variant sweep - both pair on the name and the year, and here the name and the year agree while the house does not. **This one needs the return read.**

See [[duplicate-sweep-keyed-on-house]] for the opposite failure - a pair the matchers miss because they share a house but not a year.

questions.title: Albert Nelson Bromley, architect, at 15 Newcastle Drive - and the record has his name wrong
questions.detail:
**An architect lived on the estate for at least twenty years and the record connects him to no building at all.**

Albert Nelson Bromley heads 15 Newcastle Drive in 1901 and again in 1911, giving his occupation in his own hand as **architect and surveyor, working on his own account**. A sweep of every property's history text finds **not one mention of him**.

**The record also has his middle initial wrong.** It holds #4717 as **Albert V. Bromley**, taken from the 1901 round. The 1911 schedule, written by him, says **Nelson**. That is not a small thing for an architect: **a wrong initial is exactly how a man fails to be matched to his work**, in a directory, a building list or a set of plans.

**This is the same shape as the Tarbotton find** - the Borough Surveyor who laid out The Park and turned out to be living on it. An architect in residence is worth knowing about whether or not he designed anything here.

**What to look for:**

- **Whether he designed anything in The Park.** The record credits architects on individual houses and he is not among them. Plans lodged with the borough would say.
- **His practice in Nottingham more widely.** A. N. Bromley is a name that appears on Nottingham buildings of this period; which ones wants establishing from a source rather than assumed.
- **The Architects page** should hold him once the buildings are known.

**The household, for completeness:** born at Stafford about 1851; married 32 years to Elizabeth Stephen Bromley, born Lincoln; **one child in all that time**, Kathleen, born 1879, at home in 1901 and gone by 1911 - so findable under a married name. Two servants, eleven rooms. Both husband and wife answer the nationality column *British subject by parentage*, which is odd for two people born in England and may be no more than a careful householder filling in every box.

questions.title: The Feilmanns and Max Loewenstein - Russian-born lace at 29 Newcastle Drive
questions.detail:
**Eight people at 10 Pelham Terrace in 1911, and not one of them was in the record.** It is the most unusual household of the whole 1911 round.

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| **Emilie Feilmann** | 56, widow | born **Russia**; *Resident*, **British by marriage** |
| **Gertrude Feilmann** | 35, single | **Principal of a School**, **employer** |
| **Rose Feilmann** | 34, single | **Vocalist**, own account |
| **Max Loewenstein** | 58, single, her brother | **Lace manufacturer, machine-made lace, employer**; born **Russia**, **naturalised British subject** |
| **Lilian Albert** | 40, widow, boarder | born **New South Wales** |
| three general servants | 33, 25, 21 | |

**Why this matters.** The record has held **one** person born in Russia. Here are two, heading a lace business between them, and the man is **naturalised** - which means there is a naturalisation file with a date, a former name and often a reason for coming.

**Two professional unmarried women in one house is rare anywhere in this record.** A woman who is **Principal of a school and an employer** at 35, and her sister a **professional singer** at 34. Most women in the 1911 round are wives, widows or servants. **Which school Gertrude ran should be findable in a directory**, and a vocalist leaves concert notices in the local press.

**The head's own trade is struck out on the form.** Emilie Feilmann's occupation reads *Lace Manufacturer* with *Employer* beside it, both crossed through. A widow of a lace family answered as a manufacturer and somebody - she or the enumerator - thought better of it.

**Feilmann and Loewenstein are almost certainly a Jewish family in the Nottingham lace trade**, and Nottingham's Jewish community of this period is documented. That is the obvious place to look.

**And the surname wants care.** *Feilmann* is close enough to *Flersheim* and *Hersheim*, already a known duplicate pair in this record, that a careless matcher could bring them together. They are different families.

questions.title: One province, two countries: Alsace at Pelham House in 1911
questions.detail:
**The wife gives her birthplace as *Alsace, France*. The governess gives hers as *Alsace, Germany*. Both are right.**

Alsace was French until 1871 and German from then until 1918. **Alice Lina Manning**, born about 1866, was born in France. **Anna Elizabeth Kuntz**, the governess, born about 1893, was born in Germany - in the same province. The two entries sit four lines apart on one schedule and between them date the annexation without mentioning it.

**The nationality column finishes the picture.** The wife is **British by marriage**. The governess, 18, is entered simply as **German**.

**This is April 1911.** Britain declared war on Germany in August 1914. **What became of Anna Elizabeth Kuntz is worth knowing** - German nationals in England were registered under the Aliens Restriction Act, and many were interned or repatriated. A governess of 18 in 1911 would be 21 when the war began.

**The household is Edward Laurence Manning's**, a solicitor employing others, with two children born at Beeston. **All four Mannings are already in the record** from 1921, by which time they had moved to **5 Lenton Road, Castle Bank**. So the family can be followed either side of the war, and whether the governess stayed with them is a question the 1921 return answers.

**The record spells two of them differently** - **Elise Lina** for the wife where her husband wrote Alice, and **Geoffrey Lawrence Frederic** for the son against this schedule's Geoffrey Frederic Laurence.

questions.title: John Stubbins, Stubbing and Stubbings - one man, one job, one street
questions.detail:
**Three spellings, three birthplaces, and a single career.**

| census | held as | trade | where |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1901** | #4752 John **Stubbins**, b.1854 | Corporation porter | **unfiled**, under a bare *Park Row* |
| **1911** | this schedule, 57 | **Municipal door attendant, Guildhall** | **Park Lodge, Park Row** |
| **1921** | #2239 John **Stubbing**, b.1855 | Attendant | **East Lodge, Park Row**, #413 |

**The birthplaces look like the objection and are actually the proof.** Cuckney, Holbeck and Welbeck are **three villages within a few miles of each other on the Welbeck estate** in north Nottinghamshire. A man born in one of them, asked three times in twenty years, gives whichever name he thinks the clerk will know.

**Same street, same employer, the same job dressed up a little more each decade.**

**Two things follow.**

1. **#4752 and #2239 should be merged.** The pair is exactly the *Stubbing/Stubbins* case already named in `docs/post-import-checklist.md` as one the 1901 round created, and it has never been done.
2. **Park Lodge is probably East Lodge**, #413 - and if that is confirmed, it fills 1911 for that property **and** places the **six unfiled 1901 rows** sitting under a bare *Park Row*. **Not filed yet**, because the cover says Park Lodge and the record says East Lodge, and the estate may have had more than one lodge on that road.

**His wife Maggie was born at Carlisle**, they had been married 29 years, and **no children were ever born to them**. Two rooms - the smallest dwelling in the 1911 round.

questions.title: Was John Alfred Henderson Green the Town Clerk of Nottingham?
questions.detail:
**In 1901 he is a solicitor on his own account. In 1911 he writes *Solicitor (Town Clerk)* and gives his employer as *Nottingham Corporation*.**

That is a move out of private practice into the Corporation, and the question is which post he actually held: **Town Clerk of Nottingham** is a principal office of the borough and a matter of public record, but a solicitor *in* the Town Clerk's department might write the same words. **He answers *worker* rather than *employer***, which leans towards the second reading - though a salaried Town Clerk would also be a worker.

**Easily settled** from a borough list, a directory or the local press, and worth settling: the record already holds the **Borough Surveyor** who laid out The Park and the **Postmaster of Nottingham**, and a Town Clerk would sit beside them.

**He is #4896**, held from the 1901 round as *John A. H. Green* - the full forenames come from this schedule, in his own hand.

**A second marriage.** Married nine years in 1911, so about 1902, with **no children born to that marriage**. But the 1901 household at the same house holds **Dorothy Green, 13**, his daughter, born about 1888. She is 23 by 1911 and not at home.

questions.title: Seven Castle Grove households in 1911 and not one can be filed
questions.detail:
**Seven Castle Grove households were read from the 1911 schedules and not one of them can be filed.** The property list holds **4, 5, 6, 6a and 7**. The covers give **1**, **2**, **The Lodge**, and four with **no number at all**.

| cover | head | rooms |
|---|---|---|
| **1 Castle Grove** | Harold Borden, cycle manufacturer, born San Francisco | 9 |
| **2 Castle Grove** | Herbert Herbert, late Lt-Col, Indian Medical Service | 10 |
| **The Lodge** | William Hall, coachman | 5 |
| no number | Samuel M. Taylor, **American Consul at Nottingham** | 11 |
| no number | James B. Walker, lace and lace curtain manufacturer | 12 |
| no number | Kate Mary Snook, widow, of James Snook & Co, drapers | 11 |
| no number | Frederic William Dobson, lace dyeing and dressing | 9 |

**That is 44 people with nowhere to go**, and it is not a 1911 problem: **eight rows already sit unfiled from the 1921 round** under *Castle Grove - no name or house number in 1921 census*. **Whatever fixes one fixes both.**

**The shape of the gap is clear.** The list starts at 4. **Numbers 1, 2 and 3 are missing from the record and two of them are named on covers**, so they existed. The Lodge is an eighth property again.

**Three things would settle it**, in order of cost: the **enumerator's summary book** for the piece, which lists every schedule in order with its address; a **trade directory**, which names Castle Grove householders; and the **1921 covers**, which would place the eight unfiled rows and probably name the same houses.

**Until then the seven stay on the unfiled page**, each under its own name so they can be told apart. See [[clare-valley-missing-houses]] for the same fault on another street.

questions.title: Samuel McIntire Taylor, United States Consul at Nottingham - answered
questions.detail:
**ANSWERED, by A. Hagues.** The head of an unnumbered Castle Grove household in 1911 is **Samuel McIntire Taylor (24 July 1856 - 7 December 1916)**, American lawyer, politician and diplomat, **United States Consul at Nottingham from 1910 to 1911**.
[Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_McIntire_Taylor)

**The census caught the only full year he was here.** He held Nottingham for one year. Had the count fallen either side of April 1911, he would not be in this record at all - and The Park would have housed a serving foreign consul without anything to show for it.

**A political career first, and a well-connected one.** Republican member of the **Ohio House of Representatives** from 1888, then **Secretary of State of Ohio, 1893-1897**, serving under Governor **William McKinley**. McKinley, once President, appointed him to the consular service - so the posting that brought him to Nottingham came from the man he had worked under at Columbus.

| post | years |
|---|---|
| Glasgow | 1897-1906 |
| Callao, Peru | 1906-1910 |
| **Nottingham** | **1910-1911** |
| Birmingham | 1913 until his death |

**He died in post**, of influenza, at Birmingham in December 1916, and is buried at Urbana, Ohio. Educated at Ohio Wesleyan University and the Cincinnati Law School.

**Everything on the schedule agrees.** Aged **54** on 2 April 1911, against a birth in July 1856. **Married 27 years**, so about 1884 - the year he finished law school. **One child born, one living**: Miriam, 16, born in the United States about 1895, when he was Secretary of State and before Glasgow. His wife **Myrtle A. Taylor**, 49. Two English servants.

**One lesson for the importer.** The age gives a birth year of **1857**; he was born in **July 1856** and had not had his birthday. That is precisely the fault written up at 5.5b in `docs/post-import-checklist.md`, and here it is caught against a real date rather than a suspicion. His record carries the true date.

**What is still open**: the house. **The cover gives only *Castle Grove, The Park***, and seven 1911 households on that street cannot be placed at all - see [[castle-grove-has-no-low-numbers]]. **A consul's address should be the easiest of the seven to find**, because a consulate is published: a Nottingham directory for 1910 or 1911, or the United States consular register, will give the street and number outright. **That would place one of the seven and may place its neighbours.**

questions.title: Lieutenant-Colonel Herbert Herbert FRCS, who gave his name to Herbert’s pits - answered
questions.detail:
**ANSWERED, by A. Hagues.** The head of 2 Castle Grove in 1911 is **Lieutenant-Colonel Herbert Herbert, FRCS (25 February 1865 - 19 March 1942)**, an ophthalmic surgeon of international standing. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_Herbert)

**He has an eponym.** The corneal scars left by trachoma are called **Herbert's pits**, and he was the first to describe them, in 1903. He also devised the **trap-door sclerotomy** for glaucoma, published one of the earliest papers on superficial punctate keratitis, and was **the first to record eosinophils in conjunctivitis**. His books on cataract surgery rest on **five thousand extractions performed in India**. He is counted one of the four pioneers of ophthalmology in the Indian Medical Service.

**The Nottingham question is answered, and it is the reason he is here.** He retired from the IMS in **October 1907**, returned to England in 1908, and was appointed **surgeon and then consulting surgeon to the Midland Eye Infirmary, Nottingham**. **The infirmary brought him to The Park.**

**The schedule agrees with the life at every point**, which is worth saying because it is not always so:

| the schedule | the life |
|---|---|
| aged **46** | born 25 February 1865 |
| born **Birkenhead, Cheshire** | born at **Tranmere**, part of Birkenhead |
| **married 11 years** | married 1899 |
| **4 born, 4 living** | two sons and two daughters |
| youngest born **Bombay**, aged 4 | still serving in India until October 1907 |

**His name is neither an error nor a joke.** He was born **Herbert Sherwood**, son of a barrister and judge; his surname was changed to Herbert at the age of twelve, most likely to his mother's own. **He could not change his Christian name, so he became Herbert Herbert.** Any matcher that assumes a forename and a surname must differ will mishandle him, and now there is a reason to record beside the warning.

**Commissioned 1887; major 1899; lieutenant-colonel March 1907.** Before the eye work he served in the Middle East and the Gulf of Aden, was professor at the Grant Medical College and surgeon at the Jamsetjee Jeejeebhoy Hospital in Bombay, civil surgeon at Kheda, and **wrote on the cholera epidemics of the 1890s** - including a paper read at the International Congress of Hygiene at Budapest in 1894.

**He rejoined the IMS for the First World War**, serving on hospital ships, at the Indian Hospital at Brockenhurst and in India, then settled at West Worthing and consulted to Worthing Hospital and the Sussex Eye Hospital at Brighton. Vice-president of the Ophthalmological Society of the United Kingdom. He died at Rugby, aged 77.

**What is still open is the house.** The cover gives **2 Castle Grove**, and the property list does not hold a number 2 - see [[castle-grove-has-no-low-numbers]]. **His address should be findable**: a consulting surgeon to a Nottingham infirmary is listed in the medical directories of the day, and those give a private address.
